Rarity of an effect in the population has no bearing on the mathematics of power, which depends on distance from the null value, not on how common the effect is. Power genuinely differs by effect size even with alpha held fixed, so it cannot be identical across different alternatives.
  13. The correct answer is D (Power varies continuously across the range, rising as alternatives move further from H0): When the alternative is a range rather than one fixed value, power forms a curve that typically rises as the true parameter moves further away from the null value stated in H0. Power is not constant across such a range, since alternatives closer to the null are intrinsically harder to detect than those far away. A well defined power curve can be computed at every point in a continuous range, so power is not restricted to single fixed alternatives only.
  14. The correct answer is A (An effect that is very far from H0 becomes almost certain to fall in the rejection region): When the true parameter is far from the value in H0, the sampling distribution centered at that true value places nearly all of its probability inside the rejection region, driving power toward one. Alpha is a fixed choice made by the analyst before the test and does not change automatically as the true underlying effect happens to grow. The sample size is likewise fixed by design and is not altered simply because the true effect being tested happens to be large.
  15. The correct answer is A (There is a substantial 60 percent chance of failing to detect a real effect): A power of 0.40 means beta equals 0.60, so there is a substantial sixty percent chance of a Type II error, that is, failing to detect a real effect when it genuinely exists. The five percent figure describes alpha, the Type I error rate under a true null, not the concern being raised about missing a real effect. Type I error risk remains exactly alpha regardless of how low power happens to be, so it is not eliminated by low power.
  16. The correct answer is B (Increasing the desired power while holding alpha and effect size fixed): Demanding higher power for the same alpha and effect size requires more data to sharpen the sampling distribution enough to reliably detect the effect, which increases the required sample size. Raising alpha instead makes the rejection region larger and generally reduces the sample size needed to hit a given power target. A larger assumed effect size is easier to detect and therefore actually reduces, rather than increases, the required sample size for a fixed power and alpha.

The correct answer is A (The two samples were small and the underlying population variance was large): Small samples combined with high underlying variance inflate the standard error of the difference in means, which weakens the ability of the test to distinguish a true effect from noise and lowers power. Very large samples generally increase rather than decrease power, since they shrink the standard error and sharpen detection of real differences. A high alpha of 0.20 would tend to raise power, not lower it, because it widens the rejection region considerably.

Power is a probability, not a guarantee, so even a well powered study will occasionally fail to reject purely by chance. Failing to reject a null hypothesis never proves it is exactly true, it only indicates insufficient evidence to reject it in that instance.
  19. The correct answer is B (Alpha alone does not reveal how likely the test was to detect a real problem if one existed): Alpha only bounds the chance of a false alarm, it says nothing about the chance of catching a genuine problem, which is exactly what power measures and why both figures matter together. Power is a distinct concept from the p-value, since the p-value is computed from the observed data while power is computed in advance under an assumed alternative. Power is informative in both cases, whether the test ultimately rejects or fails to reject, since it describes the design's sensitivity before the data are even seen.
  20. The correct answer is A (The probability of observing data this extreme or more, assuming H0 is true, is 0.03): A p-value is defined as the probability, computed under the assumption that H0 holds, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed. It is not the probability that H0 itself is true, since frequentist inference does not assign probabilities to fixed hypotheses in that way. It likewise is not the probability that the alternative is true, which is a common and persistent misinterpretation of what the p-value actually measures.
  21. Both values leading to rejection does not mean the underlying strength of evidence is identical, since one result sits far more extreme than the other. Meaningful comparisons between p-values below alpha are routinely made in practice to gauge relative strength of evidence.

A p-value of 0.07 does not satisfy the stated threshold, so rejecting the null here would violate the pre-committed decision rule. Failing to reject is never the same as accepting the null as definitively true, since it only reflects insufficient evidence against it at the chosen alpha.

Using only the lower tail below the observed value ignores the possibility of an equally extreme result in the opposite direction, which a two sided test must include. Squaring a tail probability has no basis in the definition of a p-value and would not yield a valid probability interpretation.

There is no fixed threshold linking p-value magnitude directly to the size of the underlying practical effect, since the two concepts answer different questions. A p-value of 0.20 is a perfectly valid and common outcome for many legitimate tests, so there is nothing mathematically impossible about it. Correct interpretation of a p-value does not depend on whether it happens to fall above or below the chosen alpha level.
  26. This uniform result holds regardless of whether the underlying test statistic itself follows a normal, t, or chi-square distribution, so claiming it must be standard normal is incorrect. Neither a chi-square nor an exponential distribution correctly describes the theoretical behavior of p-values under a true null hypothesis.
  27. Claiming the one sided value is double the two sided value reverses this well known relationship entirely. The two p-values are not identical, since the two sided version must account for extremity in both directions rather than just one.

The hypotheses being tested remain determinable from the study design itself and are unaffected by how precisely the p-value happens to be reported. Omitting the exact p-value does not invalidate the underlying test, it only limits the granularity of information conveyed to the reader.

Reversing this comparison, rejecting only when the p-value exceeds alpha, is the opposite of the correct rule and would badly misstate the test's error properties. The p-value and alpha are directly compared to reach the testing decision, so they are far from unrelated quantities.

This scenario does not eliminate false positives, it actually illustrates exactly the opposite problem arising from repeated testing. Alpha remains fixed at whatever level the analyst chose for each individual test unless a specific correction procedure is deliberately applied.

P-values remain a legitimate and commonly used tool in model comparison, they simply should not be relied upon as the sole criterion for a final decision.

A large p-value can occur with any sample size and does not by itself diagnose an inadequate sample.   34. These two phrases are deliberately kept distinct in rigorous statistical writing precisely because conflating them overstates what the test procedure can actually demonstrate. Accepting the null outright is a conceptual overreach rather than any kind of Type I error, which instead refers to a false rejection.

The value 1.96 instead corresponds to a two sided test at alpha equals 0.05, splitting 0.025 into each of the two tails, which does not match this one sided scenario. The value 2.576 corresponds to a two sided test at alpha equals 0.01, where only half of 0.01 sits in each tail, again not matching the one sided case described.

Claiming a z-test can never be applied to skewed populations ignores this large sample justification entirely. A chi-square test addresses a fundamentally different question, typically about a population variance or a goodness of fit comparison, not a direct test of the mean. Valid tests of the mean certainly exist when sigma is unknown, the t-test being the exact procedure designed specifically for that situation, particularly in smaller samples.

A positive z statistic alone does not indicate significance, what matters is whether its magnitude clears the relevant critical value threshold. Comparing against the one sided critical value of 1.28 is not appropriate here since the stated test is explicitly two sided rather than one sided.

Simply averaging the two variance terms ignores how each is separately scaled by its own respective sample size before combination. Subtracting the variance terms would be mathematically invalid, since variances of independent quantities add together when computing the variance of their difference, they never subtract.

Unequal sample sizes and large population standard deviations are both readily accommodated by the general two sample z-test formula and do not undermine independence.

Claiming the restricted model always achieves a strictly larger likelihood reverses this fundamental nesting relationship entirely. Log-likelihood values are commonly negative numbers, since likelihoods themselves are probabilities between zero and one, so their logarithms are typically negative, not guaranteed positive.

A two sample t-test compares means between two independent samples of data, it is not designed to compare the fit of two nested parametric distributional models. A chi-square test of independence addresses association between two categorical variables, an entirely different question from comparing nested severity distribution models, and the Anderson-Darling test compares a single fitted distribution to raw sample data rather than directly comparing two competing fitted models to each other.

Numerical difference alone from the hypothesized value does not automatically trigger rejection, since sampling variability must be accounted for.

Sample size adequacy is a separate consideration and this outcome alone says nothing about whether 40 was too small.

The problem exists regardless of sample size and does not guarantee any particular test statistic outcome.

A goodness-of-fit test evaluates an entire distributional shape rather than a single variance parameter.

  46. The correct answer is C (it blends the insured's own observed experience with a broader class based rate through the credibility): Pure experience rating relies entirely on an insured's own observed data while pure manual rating relies entirely on class level rates, and the Bayesian credibility weighted posterior mean sits between these two extremes by blending both sources according to the credibility factor Z. It does not assign full weight to only one source in general, and it does not discard both sources in favor of an arbitrary constant.

Practice Test 19 Answer Key

  1. The correct answer is B (Insured B has substantially more observed exposure or claims experience than Insured A does): Since both insureds share the identical prior, the difference in credibility factors must come from the data side of the formula, meaning Insured B has accumulated substantially more exposure or claims experience than Insured A, giving Insured B's own data more relative weight. Both insureds share the same prior by assumption, Insured A's smaller Z indicates lower rather than higher reliability of its own experience, and credibility is directly tied to the amount of exposure observed.
  2. The correct answer is A (the posterior mean, since it minimizes expected squared error loss over the posterior): Under squared error loss, the Bayes estimator that minimizes expected loss with respect to the posterior distribution is the posterior mean, a standard result in Bayesian decision theory. The posterior mode minimizes a different loss function, namely zero one loss in the continuous limit, the prior mean ignores the observed data entirely, and the maximum observed value is not a principled minimizer under this loss.
  3. The correct answer is D (the posterior mean typically exceeds the posterior mode because the long right tail pulls the mean): For a right skewed distribution, the long tail on the high side pulls the mean above the mode, which sits at the peak of the density, so the posterior mean typically exceeds the posterior mode in this setting. The two are identical only for symmetric unimodal distributions such as the Normal, the described relationship is reversed from what is typical here, and both quantities remain fully computable for a skewed posterior.
  4. The correct answer is A (a zero one loss function that penalizes any nonzero estimation error equally, in the continuous limit): The MAP estimate is optimal under a zero one loss function, which assigns a fixed penalty to any nonzero error regardless of magnitude, and in the continuous limit this loss is minimized by the mode of the posterior distribution. Squared error loss is instead minimized by the posterior mean, absolute error loss is minimized by the posterior median, and an asymmetric loss favoring one direction of error leads to neither the mean nor the mode in general.
  5. The correct answer is A (all three measures coincide at the identical single central value of the distribution): For a symmetric unimodal distribution such as the Normal, the mean, median, and mode all coincide at the same central point of symmetry, which is why point estimate choice matters less for this particular family than for skewed posteriors. The described strict inequalities do not hold under symmetry, and all three measures remain simultaneously well defined and computable.
  6. The correct answer is C (a posterior mode value of approximately 1.00 for this parameter): The mode of a Gamma(alpha, beta) distribution with alpha greater than one is (alpha minus 1) divided by beta, so here it is (3 minus 1) divided by 2, which equals 1.00. This differs from the posterior mean of alpha divided by beta, which would be 3 divided by 2, or 1.50, illustrating that the mean and mode diverge for a skewed Gamma posterior.
  7. The correct answer is C (a posterior mode value of approximately 0.33 for this parameter): The posterior mean is alpha divided by beta, or 6 divided by 3, equal to 2.00, and the posterior mode is (alpha minus 1) divided by beta, or 5 divided by 3, approximately 1.67, so the difference is 2.00 minus 1.67, which is approximately 0.33. This nonzero gap between the mean and mode reflects the right skewness of the Gamma distribution.
  8. The correct answer is B (the median is less sensitive to the extreme values in a long right tail): For a heavily right skewed distribution, a small number of extreme large values can pull the mean substantially upward, while the median, defined as the fiftieth percentile, is comparatively robust to those extreme values, making it a more stable summary in some practical reporting contexts. The median is not generally equal to the mean under skewness, it remains fully computable for any continuous distribution, and it does not generally coincide with the mode either.
  9. The correct answer is D (the posterior median, since it minimizes expected absolute error loss over the posterior): The Bayes estimator under absolute error loss is the posterior median, a classical result paralleling how the posterior mean is optimal under squared error loss. The posterior mean instead minimizes squared error loss, the posterior mode minimizes zero one loss, and posterior variance is a measure of spread rather than a point estimate at all.
  10. The correct answer is A (as sample size grows large, the posterior becomes increasingly concentrated and approximately symmetric): With a large sample, the posterior distribution tends to become sharply concentrated around the true parameter value and increasingly approximately Normal in shape by asymptotic theory, and for such symmetric concentrated distributions the mean and mode nearly coincide. The posterior does not become uniform with more data, the prior's relative influence shrinks rather than grows with larger samples, and the mean and mode converge rather than diverge as the sample grows.
  11. The correct answer is B (there is a 90 percent posterior probability that lambda lies within the stated interval): A Bayesian credible interval has the direct probabilistic interpretation that, given the observed data and the chosen prior, there is a 90 percent posterior probability the parameter lambda lies within the stated bounds. It does not describe future observed data directly, the repeated sampling interpretation describes a frequentist confidence interval instead, and it makes no claim that lambda exactly equals the posterior mean.
  12. The correct answer is A (if the sampling procedure were repeated many times): The correct frequentist interpretation of a confidence interval concerns the long run behavior of the procedure across repeated samples, namely that about 90 percent of intervals constructed this way would capture the true fixed lambda, since lambda itself is not treated as random. Claiming a direct probability statement about this one specific interval containing lambda is the Bayesian interpretation, not the frequentist one, it does not describe individual claim counts, and it makes no claim of certainty about the sample mean.
  13. The correct answer is C (the frequentist approach treats the parameter as fixed while the Bayesian approach treats it as random): The fundamental distinction is philosophical rather than purely numerical, the frequentist framework treats the unknown parameter as a fixed constant and the interval as random across repeated samples, while the Bayesian framework treats the parameter itself as a random variable with a genuine probability distribution given the data. The two approaches can use the identical sample size, one is not universally wider than the other, and the Bayesian interval depends heavily on the observed data through the posterior.
  14. The correct answer is B (an equal tailed credible interval, cutting equal probability from each tail): An equal tailed credible interval is formed by cutting equal probability, alpha over 2, from each tail of the posterior distribution, which is a simple and commonly used construction. A highest posterior density interval instead selects the shortest interval containing the desired posterior probability, which need not have equal tail probabilities, and the other two options describe entirely different, non Bayesian interval constructions.
  15. The correct answer is D (the HPD interval is generally shorter than the equal tailed interval for the same coverage probability): The HPD interval is specifically constructed to be the shortest possible interval achieving the desired posterior probability, so for a skewed posterior it is generally shorter than or equal to the equal tailed interval, which instead fixes equal tail probabilities without regard to minimizing overall length. The described reversed relationship does not generally hold, the two intervals coincide only for symmetric posteriors, and the HPD interval remains computable for skewed posteriors.
  16. The correct answer is B (as sample size grows, the likelihood dominates any reasonable prior): With a large sample, the likelihood increasingly dominates the influence of a reasonable prior, so the resulting posterior becomes driven almost entirely by the data, and this large sample behavior parallels the asymptotic behavior underlying frequentist confidence intervals, causing the two interval types to converge numerically. The two do not diverge with more data, a confidence interval does not collapse to a single point except in a limiting sense tied to shrinking width, and the Bayesian interval remains firmly tied to the observed data throughout.
  17. The correct answer is D (the credible interval reflects the probability of the parameter itself given the data actually observed): The clearest distinction is that a credible interval makes a direct probability statement about the parameter conditional on the specific data actually observed, unlike a confidence interval, which instead describes the long run performance of the interval construction procedure across hypothetical repeated samples. It is not restricted to symmetric distributions, it carries no minimum sample size requirement of thirty, and it is a statement about the parameter's posterior distribution rather than merely a raw data range.
  18. The correct answer is A (not necessarily, since a wider interval may simply reflect genuinely limited or highly variable data): A wider credible interval at a fixed probability level generally reflects greater remaining uncertainty, which can arise simply from limited sample size or genuinely high data variability rather than from any flaw in the chosen prior. It does not automatically indicate an incorrect prior, it does not automatically indicate a misspecified likelihood, and interval width is directly influenced by how much and how variable the observed data is.

The other values understate or overstate this standard Normal based multiplier.

  22. A factor of 4 would apply if standard error scaled directly with the inverse of sample size rather than its square root, and the standard error certainly does not stay unchanged or shrink by the full factor of 40,000.
  23. Changing the seed's numerical precision, rounding output values, or discarding trials at random are not recognized variance reduction techniques and can actually harm estimator quality.
  24. When a closed form solution is readily available it is usually preferred over simulation for both speed and precision, Monte Carlo inherently relies on random number generation rather than avoiding it, and no such blanket regulatory prohibition is a standard actuarial exam premise.
  25. The correct answer is C (the precision of the estimated percentile generally improves as the number of simulated trials increases): As with most Monte Carlo based estimates, increasing the number of simulated trials generally reduces the sampling variability of the estimated percentile, improving its precision, although extreme tail percentiles typically require substantially more trials than a central quantity like the mean to achieve comparable precision. Precision is not unrelated to trial count, it does not systematically worsen with more trials, and the specific seed value used does not meaningfully drive overall estimator precision.
  26. It does not require fewer trials by itself, it does not remove the need for distributional assumptions in setting up the simulation, and it is a variance reduction technique rather than a bias correction technique.

Applying F directly to U rather than its inverse, reversing the roles of X and U, or dividing by F(U) do not correctly implement the inverse transform method.

The other formulas misplace the lambda parameter or apply an incorrect algebraic inversion of the exponential cumulative distribution function.

  30. The other formulas do not correctly invert the Uniform cumulative distribution function.

Choosing 2 stops too early since F(2) has not yet reached U, choosing 1 stops far too early, and choosing 4 overshoots past the correct smallest qualifying value.

The Pareto distribution does have a well defined cumulative distribution function, the inverse transform method works for many unbounded distributions such as the Pareto and Exponential, and the Pareto is a continuous rather than a discrete distribution.

Substituting an unrelated Normal distribution changes the target distribution entirely, replacing the simulation with a purely deterministic calculation defeats its purpose, and exact analytical integration is often precisely what is infeasible in these complex cases.
  39. The method still relies fundamentally on uniform draws, it applies to both continuous and discrete distributions, and simulated values retain genuine variability rather than having zero variance.

Sampling without replacement or with a smaller size is not the bootstrap procedure, fitting a parametric distribution first describes the parametric rather than nonparametric bootstrap, and simply repeating the original data provides no random variability to estimate.
  41.   42. The 1st and 99th percentiles would instead form a 98 percent interval, the 10th and 90th would form an 80 percent interval, and the minimum and maximum values do not correspond to a fixed confidence level.
  43. When the true parametric family is confidently known, a parametric approach is often more efficient, an extremely small sample size actually limits the reliability of any bootstrap method rather than favoring it, and there is no meaningful statistic to bootstrap when only the raw sample size itself is of interest.
  44. It still requires the original observed data to resample from, it provides no guarantee that the sample median exactly equals the true population median, and it does not universally produce narrower intervals than every classical method.

The bootstrap does not reveal the true population percentile with certainty, it is not simply a count of claims exceeding a threshold in the original data, and it does not identify the true parametric family generating the data.

The resample does not reproduce every original observation with certainty, 50.0 percent is not the correct asymptotic figure, and 36.8 percent is instead the fraction of distinct observations expected to be entirely left out.

Original sample size is not irrelevant to bootstrap reliability, reliability does not generally worsen as the original sample grows, and there is no fixed universal minimum such as exactly 1,000 observations required for the bootstrap to be usable.

This exceeds the prior of 0.25 because a claim is relatively more likely under the high-risk hypothesis.
  3. The correct answer is A (0.6667): The marginal probability of a claim equals 0.40(0.30) + 0.60(0.10) = 0.12 + 0.06 = 0.18. The observed claim shifts belief upward from the 0.40 prior because claims occur three times more often under high-risk.

The posterior probability that the policy belongs to the middle tier is 0.06 divided by 0.19, which equals 0.3158. This is only slightly above the prior of 0.30 since the middle tier's claim rate is close to the portfolio average.
  5. The correct answer is A (0.3077): The prior odds of fraud are 0.10/0.90, which equals 1/9. Multiplying by the likelihood ratio of 4 gives posterior odds of 4/9. Converting odds to probability gives (4/9) divided by (1 + 4/9), which equals 4/13 or approximately 0.3077, a meaningful increase from the 0.10 prior.
  6. The correct answer is B (0.7200): The prior odds are 0.30/0.70, or 3/7. Multiplying sequentially by likelihood ratios 2 and then 3 gives combined odds of 3/7 times 6, which equals 18/7. Converting to a probability gives (18/7) divided by (1 + 18/7), which equals 0.72. Updating with each piece of evidence in sequence gives the same result as updating once with the combined likelihood ratio of 6.

Ignoring the normalizing constant is valid for finding the posterior's shape but not its exact probabilities.
  8. It does not affect the shape of the posterior, only its total probability mass.
  9. Treating every point identically wastes information and inflates the variance of the coefficient estimates. GLMs address this through the mean-variance relationship built into the chosen distribution.

A GLM naturally incorporates a prior weight tied to exposure, so variance scales inversely with exposure.

This is why b(theta) is central to identifying the mean-variance relationship for any exponential family member.

Practice Test 23 Answer Key

  1. The correct answer is D (It allows a single estimation algorithm and set of diagnostic tools to apply across many response): Because the normal, Poisson, gamma, and binomial distributions all fit the common exponential family form, the same iteratively reweighted least squares algorithm, the same deviance based goodness of fit measures, and the same standard error formulas apply regardless of the distribution chosen. This shared structure lets actuaries move between frequency, severity, and probability models using one consistent toolkit. The practitioner still must choose the distribution appropriate to the data.

This is the identity link case, where the natural parameter and the mean coincide exactly. This pairing is why the identity link is the canonical link for the normal distribution.
  3. The correct answer is C (theta equals the natural logarithm of the quantity mu divided by one minus mu): Writing the binomial probability mass function in exponential family form and collecting the term multiplying y gives theta equal to the logit of mu, the log odds mu over one minus mu. This is the quantity known as the canonical parameter for the binomial distribution. The corresponding cumulant function is b(theta) equal to log(1 plus exp(theta)), whose derivative recovers mu.
  4. The correct answer is C (Var(Y) equals mu itself, since b''(theta) equals exp(theta) which equals mu): Differentiating b(theta) equal to exp(theta) twice gives b''(theta) equal to exp(theta), which equals mu because theta equals log(mu). With a(phi) equal to one for the Poisson distribution, Var(Y) equals a(phi) times b''(theta), which reduces to exactly mu. This confirms the equidispersion property of the Poisson distribution, where the mean and variance are always equal.
  5. The correct answer is A (V(mu) equals mu squared, since b''(theta) equals one over theta squared which equals mu squared): Differentiating b(theta) equal to negative log(negative theta) twice gives b''(theta) equal to one over theta squared. Substituting theta equal to negative 1 over mu gives mu squared. This quadratic variance function is the defining feature of the gamma distribution and explains why gamma models suit severity data whose spread grows proportionally with claim size.
  6. The correct answer is D (It specifies which exponential family distribution governs the variability of the response variable): The random component of a GLM specifies the probability distribution assumed for the response, such as Poisson for counts or gamma for severities, together with its associated variance function. This choice determines how the likelihood is constructed and how observations are weighted during estimation. It is distinct from the systematic component, which specifies the predictors themselves, and from the link function, which connects the two.
  7. What differs from OLS is what happens to eta next, since the GLM passes eta through the inverse link function to obtain the fitted mean rather than treating eta itself as the mean. This linear-in-parameters structure is what makes the systematic component tractable to estimate.
  8. Inverting the link then maps eta back to a valid mu. Ordinary linear regression has no such step because it assumes the mean is already unrestricted, which is exactly the identity link case.
  9. The systematic component can keep the same or similar predictors, and the log link is commonly retained for severity models too since it also keeps fitted means positive. This illustrates how the three GLM components can be mixed and matched to fit the data at hand.

This exponentiation is exactly why the log link guarantees a strictly positive fitted mean regardless of the sign of eta, a property essential for modeling claim counts.

Actuaries commonly favor the log link over the canonical inverse link in practice because the log link guarantees positivity and produces multiplicative rating factors that are easier to interpret.

This makes sense intuitively because a linear predictor of zero corresponds to even odds between lapsing and not lapsing, the midpoint of the probability scale.

This is why the logit link is the canonical and strongly preferred choice for binomial response variables.

This flexible family is a natural extension of the standard exponential family members covered in an introductory GLM treatment.
  38. The correct answer is A (The Poisson distribution structurally forces the mean and variance to be exactly equal): Because the Poisson variance function is V(mu) equal to mu with a(phi) fixed at one, the Poisson distribution has no mechanism to represent variance exceeding the mean, a pattern called overdispersion that is extremely common in real claim count data. When the sample variance is noticeably larger than the sample mean, this signals the Poisson assumption is too restrictive, and a negative binomial distribution, which adds an extra dispersion parameter, or a quasi-Poisson model with an estimated phi, is often used instead. This is a routine diagnostic check actuaries run whenever fitting frequency models to real claim count data.
  39. The correct answer is C (The lognormal distribution does not belong to the exponential family in the mean parameterization typically used): Although both distributions are positive and right skewed, the lognormal distribution is not itself a member of the exponential family when parameterized directly by its mean on the original scale, so it cannot be fit using the standard GLM machinery described here without first applying a logarithmic transformation to the response and then using ordinary linear regression on the transformed scale. The gamma distribution, in contrast, is a genuine exponential family member and fits directly into the GLM framework with its own natural mean parameterization. This distinction matters when an actuary chooses between transforming the response versus using a GLM link function.
  40. The correct answer is C (Because setting the derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to theta equal to zero produces exactly b'(theta) equal to y): Differentiating the single-observation log-likelihood with respect to theta gives (y minus b'(theta)) over a(phi), and setting this derivative to zero for the maximum yields b'(theta) equal to y. Since b'(theta) also equals the mean mu by definition of the cumulant function, this shows the maximum likelihood estimate of theta for a single observation makes the fitted mean match the observed value exactly, a saturated model result. In an actual GLM with multiple observations sharing common coefficients through the linear predictor, this exact match is generally not achievable for every observation simultaneously, which is precisely what the deviance measures.
  41. The correct answer is D (Linear refers to the linear predictor eta being a linear combination of the regression coefficients): The word linear in generalized linear model refers specifically to the systematic component, the linear predictor eta, which is constructed as a weighted sum of the predictors with the coefficients entering linearly, exactly as in ordinary regression. The link function can introduce substantial nonlinearity into the relationship between the predictors and the fitted mean mu itself, such as an exponential curve under the log link, without changing the fact that eta remains linear in the coefficients. This distinction between linearity in the coefficients and nonlinearity in the mean is central to understanding GLM terminology correctly.
  42. The correct answer is C (Both links map the real line to the zero to one interval, but only the logit link gives coefficients a direct odds-ratio interpretation): Both the logit and probit links are valid choices for a binomial random component and both transform the unrestricted linear predictor into a fitted probability between zero and one, typically giving similar fitted probabilities across the middle of the range. The key practical difference is that the logit link, being the canonical link, allows coefficients to be interpreted directly on the log-odds scale, with exponentiated coefficients giving multiplicative odds ratios, an interpretation the probit link does not offer as naturally. This interpretability advantage is why the logit link is used far more often in actuarial practice.
  43. The correct answer is C (Because the score equations for a GLM are generally nonlinear except in the normal, identity link special case): Except in the special case of a normal random component with the identity link, the score equations that define the maximum likelihood estimates involve the fitted mean mu through a nonlinear link function, so there is no closed form algebraic solution for the coefficients as there is in OLS. Iteratively reweighted least squares repeatedly linearizes the problem around a current estimate, updates weights based on the current fitted values, and re-solves a weighted least squares problem, converging to the maximum likelihood solution. This iterative structure is a defining computational feature distinguishing GLM estimation from simple OLS.
  44. The correct answer is D (The Tweedie distribution places positive probability exactly at zero while remaining continuous for positive values): For variance power p strictly between one and two, the Tweedie distribution arises as a compound Poisson gamma process, meaning it has a genuine probability mass at exactly zero, representing policies with no claims, combined with a continuous gamma-shaped distribution over positive pure premium values. This structural match to actual pure premium data, which similarly has a spike at zero and a continuous positive tail, is the key reason some actuaries model pure premium directly with a single Tweedie GLM rather than fitting separate frequency and severity models. The compound structure also makes the Tweedie a natural bridge between purely frequency-based and purely severity-based modeling approaches.
  45. The correct answer is C (The partial derivative term partial mu over partial eta cancels exactly with the variance term): Under the canonical link, the natural parameter theta equals the linear predictor eta directly, and because Var(Y) equals a(phi) times b''(theta), while partial mu over partial eta also equals b''(theta) under the canonical link, these two quantities cancel in the score equation. What remains is the simpler sum over observations of (y minus mu) times x_j divided by a(phi), which is exactly the form referenced earlier in this material. This cancellation is the concrete mathematical simplification that makes canonical links computationally convenient.

Practice Test 24 Answer Key

  1. The correct answer is C (The binomial distribution correctly bounds the response between zero and one and captures variance shrinking near the boundaries as the mean approaches either extreme): A renewal proportion is fundamentally bounded between zero and one, and the binomial distribution's variance function mu times (1 minus mu) naturally reflects that proportions near the extremes have less variance than proportions near one half. The normal distribution instead assumes constant variance regardless of the mean and places no structural bound on the fitted mean at all, which can produce nonsensical fitted proportions outside the zero to one range. This structural match between the binomial distribution and the bounded, variance-shrinking nature of proportion data is the key justification for its use here.
  2. The correct answer is A (a(phi) equals one, since the Bernoulli distribution has no free dispersion parameter to estimate): Just as with the Poisson distribution, the Bernoulli distribution has only a single free parameter, the success probability mu, with no separate scale parameter, so a(phi) is set to one by convention when writing its density in exponential family form. This matches the general rule that discrete distributions arising from counting processes with a fixed underlying probability structure tend to have their dispersion fixed at one, in contrast to continuous distributions like the gamma or normal which carry a genuine free dispersion parameter. Recognizing this pattern helps actuaries correctly write out the exponential family form for any Bernoulli-based response.
  3. The correct answer is C (The fitted probability mu is approximately 0.20, obtained by inverting the logit link formula): Inverting the logit link gives mu equal to exp(eta) over (1 plus exp(eta)). Substituting exp(eta) approximately equal to 0.25 gives mu approximately equal to 0.25 over 1.25, which equals exactly 0.20. This illustrates how a negative linear predictor under the logit link corresponds to a fitted probability below one half, consistent with negative log odds implying the event is less likely than not.
  4. The correct answer is A (The binomial variance function shrinks toward zero as mu approaches either boundary): Because V(mu) equal to mu times (1 minus mu) approaches zero as mu approaches either zero or one, observations with extreme fitted probabilities are treated by the estimation algorithm as carrying less inherent noise, which is exactly the correct statistical behavior since an event that is nearly certain or nearly impossible has little remaining uncertainty about its outcome. This built in down-weighting near the boundaries is a structural feature of the binomial variance function that keeps the model well behaved in these regions, unlike a constant variance assumption which would treat every observation identically regardless of its fitted probability. This structural property is one reason the binomial GLM tends to fit probability data more reliably near the boundaries.
  5. The correct answer is A (The variance function appears in the denominator, so larger variance observations receive proportionally less weight): Because Var(Y) sits in the denominator of the generic score equation, an observation whose fitted mean implies a larger variance under the chosen distribution automatically contributes less weight to the estimating equations than an observation with a smaller implied variance. This is the precise mechanism through which GLMs correct the inefficiency problem that plain OLS suffers from when variance is not constant across observations. Choosing the right random component, and hence the right variance function, is therefore central to obtaining efficient coefficient estimates from real insurance data.
  6. The correct answer is C (Because phi only enters the variance formula and the score equations for the coefficients): Since a(phi) is typically taken to equal phi divided by a known prior weight, it appears as a constant multiplicative scale factor in the score equations for the coefficients and cancels out of the equations that determine the maximum likelihood estimates of beta. This means the coefficients can be estimated first without knowing phi, and phi can then be estimated afterward from the resulting residual deviance or Pearson chi-squared statistic. This separation simplifies the overall GLM fitting process considerably.
  7. The correct answer is A (The negative binomial distribution belongs to the exponential family only when its dispersion parameter is fixed and known): When the negative binomial's extra shape or dispersion parameter is treated as fixed and known rather than estimated jointly with the mean, the resulting distribution can be written in the standard exponential family form and fit using ordinary GLM machinery. If that extra parameter must instead be estimated simultaneously with the regression coefficients, the model falls outside the strict single-parameter exponential family framework, though software packages still commonly fit it using an extension of GLM methods. This nuance is why negative binomial models are sometimes described as requiring special estimation routines beyond a textbook GLM.
  8. The correct answer is D (Modeling the severity, meaning the dollar amount, of an individual claim once it has occurred): The gamma distribution's strictly positive support and its variance function growing with the square of the mean make it the standard actuarial choice for modeling claim severity, where larger expected claims naturally carry proportionally larger variability. The Poisson distribution is instead the standard choice for claim frequency counts, and the binomial distribution is the standard choice for modeling proportions or probabilities such as litigation rates. Matching the correct exponential family member to the correct type of insurance response is a foundational skill emphasized throughout introductory GLM material.
  9. The correct answer is B (Phi determines the overall scale of the variance while V(mu) determines how that variance changes): The variance function V(mu) captures the shape of the relationship between the mean and the variance, such as constant, linear, or quadratic growth, while the dispersion parameter phi acts as a single multiplicative scale factor applied uniformly across all observations regardless of their mean. Two datasets could share the identical variance function shape, say both gamma distributed, yet have very different overall variability, which is exactly the distinction phi captures. Separating shape from scale in this way is what allows the exponential family to describe such a wide range of distributions with one unified formula.
  10. The correct answer is A (This indicates the actual variance in the data is roughly 2.4 times larger than the Poisson): The ratio of the Pearson chi-squared statistic to its degrees of freedom is a standard estimate of phi, and under a strict Poisson assumption this ratio should be close to one since phi is fixed at one by convention. A ratio of 2.4 signals overdispersion, meaning the observed variability in claim counts exceeds what the Poisson mean-variance relationship alone predicts. Actuaries commonly respond by estimating phi freely in a quasi-Poisson model, which inflates standard errors appropriately without changing the point estimates of the coefficients themselves.
  11. The correct answer is A (The standard errors are scaled by the square root of the estimated phi): Because the coefficient point estimates in a GLM do not depend on phi under the standard convention, switching from a fixed phi of one to an estimated phi leaves the coefficients themselves unchanged, but the standard error formulas involve the square root of phi as a multiplicative factor. When phi is estimated to be greater than one, reflecting overdispersion, the standard errors widen accordingly, which correctly reflects the additional uncertainty present in overdispersed data. Ignoring overdispersion and reporting the narrower strict Poisson standard errors would understate the true uncertainty and could lead to overconfident conclusions about which rating variables are statistically significant.
  12. The correct answer is D (Because V(mu) equal to mu squared for the gamma distribution makes the standard deviation directly proportional): With V(mu) equal to mu squared, the variance is phi times mu squared, so the standard deviation is the square root of phi times mu, meaning the standard deviation grows exactly in proportion to the mean itself. Dividing the standard deviation by the mean then gives the square root of phi, a constant that does not depend on mu at all, exactly matching the constant coefficient of variation property often observed in claim severity data. This structural property is a key reason actuaries reach for the gamma distribution whenever severity data show roughly proportional relative variability across different size classes.
  13. The correct answer is C (A normal GLM cannot represent any dependence of variance on the mean since its implied variance): Because V(mu) equal to one under the normal distribution, the implied variance Var(Y) equal to phi does not vary with the fitted mean mu at all, regardless of how the actual data behave. If the true underlying data show variance growing with the mean, as insurance claim data commonly do, a normal GLM will systematically mis-weight observations, treating high-mean and low-mean observations as equally informative when they are not. This is precisely the limitation that choosing a Poisson, gamma, or binomial random component, each with a mean-dependent variance function, is designed to overcome.
  14. The correct answer is C (The implied variance equals 200,000, obtained by multiplying phi by the square of the fitted mean): Substituting V(mu) equal to mu squared into Var(Y) equal to phi times V(mu) gives Var(Y) equal to phi times mu squared. With mu equal to 500, mu squared equals 250,000, and multiplying by phi equal to 0.8 gives 200,000 exactly. This calculation shows how the fitted mean and the estimated dispersion parameter combine directly to produce the implied variance for any individual observation under a gamma GLM.
  15. The correct answer is C (The implied standard deviation equals approximately 3.46, obtained by taking the square root of the fitted): Under the Poisson mean-variance relationship, Var(Y) equals phi times mu, and with phi equal to one this reduces to Var(Y) equal to mu directly, so Var(Y) equals 12 here. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and the square root of 12 is approximately 3.46. This illustrates the characteristic Poisson property that relative variability, the standard deviation divided by the mean, shrinks as the mean grows larger, since the square root grows more slowly than the mean itself.
  16. The correct answer is D (Under the Poisson distribution the coefficient of variation shrinks toward zero as mu grows): For the Poisson distribution the standard deviation grows as the square root of mu while the mean grows as mu itself, so their ratio, the coefficient of variation, shrinks toward zero as mu increases, meaning large expected counts become relatively more predictable. For the gamma distribution the standard deviation grows exactly proportionally to mu, so the coefficient of variation, the square root of phi, remains constant regardless of the size of mu. This contrast explains why large expected claim counts are relatively more predictable than large expected claim severities under these two standard actuarial distributions.
  17. The correct answer is C (Because it lets a single formula flexibly capture how variance changes with the mean across many distributions): By separating the variance into a distribution-specific shape term V(mu) and a scale term phi, this single general formula can represent constant variance for the normal distribution, linearly growing variance for the Poisson distribution, quadratically growing variance for the gamma distribution, and bell shaped variance for the binomial distribution, all within one unified structure. OLS instead assumes constant variance unconditionally, which as demonstrated repeatedly throughout this material, mismatches the actual behavior of frequency, severity, and probability data commonly encountered in insurance applications. This flexibility is precisely what makes the GLM framework so widely adopted in actuarial rating and reserving work.
  18. The correct answer is C (The random component must be fixed as normal and the link function fixed as identity): OLS emerges from the GLM framework precisely when the random component is chosen to be the normal distribution, giving constant variance V(mu) equal to one, and the link function is chosen to be the identity, meaning mu equals eta directly with no transformation. Under these two specific choices, maximizing the normal log-likelihood becomes mathematically equivalent to minimizing the sum of squared residuals, recovering the familiar OLS normal equations exactly. The systematic component, the linear predictor itself, remains the same linear combination of predictors used in any GLM and does not need to be restricted further to obtain this equivalence.
  19. The correct answer is C (Because minimizing squared error and maximizing the normal likelihood under the identity link are mathematically identical): The normal log-likelihood, after dropping terms that do not depend on the coefficients, reduces to negative one half over sigma squared times the sum of squared residuals, so maximizing this log-likelihood is exactly equivalent to minimizing the sum of squared residuals since sigma squared is a positive constant with respect to the coefficients. This is not a coincidence but a direct algebraic consequence of the normal density's functional form combined with the identity link. This equivalence is the formal proof, rather than merely an analogy, that OLS is a genuine special case nested within the broader GLM framework.
  20. The correct answer is B (Because non-normal GLMs better match the actual shape, range, and variance structure of insurance data): Although OLS is nested within the GLM framework as the normal, identity link special case, this does not make it equally suitable for every dataset, since the normal distribution's unbounded range and constant variance are frequently poor matches for claim counts, severities, and probabilities. Choosing a Poisson, gamma, or binomial random component with an appropriate link function generally produces a model that better reflects the true data generating process, leading to more efficient estimates and more sensible fitted values. The broader GLM framework exists precisely to give actuaries this flexibility beyond the restrictive special case that OLS represents.
  21. The correct answer is D (Yes, because the identity link is the canonical link for the normal distribution): Since the identity link is exactly the canonical link for the normal distribution, the general result that canonical link score equations simplify to the sum over observations of (y minus mu) times x_j divided by a(phi) applies directly, and because a(phi) is a positive constant with respect to the coefficients, this reduces to the standard OLS normal equations. This confirms that the familiar closed form OLS estimator is not a separate special technique but rather the direct consequence of applying the general GLM canonical link machinery to the normal distribution case. This connection is a key unifying insight tested throughout introductory GLM material.
  22. The correct answer is D (Weighted least squares corresponds to a normal GLM with the identity link and prior weights incorporated): Just as ordinary least squares is the unweighted normal GLM under the identity link, weighted least squares arises when known prior weights are incorporated into the dispersion function a(phi), so that a(phi) equals phi divided by the prior weight for each observation, exactly mirroring the role prior weights play in the general GLM variance formula. Observations with larger known variance, and hence smaller weight, contribute proportionally less to the score equations, precisely the intended behavior of weighted least squares. This shows the GLM framework naturally subsumes both unweighted and weighted linear regression as special cases of the same underlying structure.
  23. The correct answer is D (Because presenting both under maximum likelihood reveals that OLS estimation is a specific instance): Framing OLS within the maximum likelihood paradigm, rather than treating it as a separate least squares technique, shows that the same underlying estimation logic, choosing coefficients that maximize the probability of observing the data given the model, applies uniformly whether the random component is normal, Poisson, gamma, or binomial. This unification is precisely why actuaries can learn one set of estimation principles, diagnostic tools, and inference procedures and apply them consistently across the very different types of response variables encountered in insurance work. Understanding OLS as a GLM special case is therefore not merely a mathematical curiosity but a foundational organizing concept for the entire subject.
  24. The correct answer is B (Because the log link makes the fitted mean a nonlinear function of the predictor): Under the log link, mu equals exp(eta) rather than mu equal to eta directly as under the identity link, so even though the random component remains normal, the relationship between the predictors and the fitted mean is nonlinear and multiplicative rather than the simple linear relationship OLS assumes. This demonstrates that the OLS special case requires both the correct random component and the correct link function together, since changing either ingredient alone produces a genuinely different model with different fitted values and different score equations, even while remaining a valid GLM in its own right. This example shows the log link and identity link are not interchangeable even under an otherwise identical random component.
  25. The correct answer is B (The choice of random component, extending beyond the normal distribution, and the choice of link function): The entire generalization from OLS to the broader GLM framework rests on relaxing exactly these two restrictive assumptions, allowing the random component to be any member of the exponential family with a variance structure appropriate to the data, and allowing the link function to be any monotonic, differentiable function suited to the response's natural range rather than forcing the identity link. Holding both choices fixed at normal and identity recovers OLS exactly as a nested special case, while varying either or both produces the much richer family of models actuaries actually use for frequency, severity, and probability data. This two dimensional generalization is the core conceptual takeaway of an introductory treatment of generalized linear models.
  26. The correct answer is A (Because the chosen distribution simultaneously determines the likelihood used for estimation and the variance function): Selecting a random component fixes both the shape of the log-likelihood being maximized and the variance function V(mu) that enters the denominator of the score equations, so a poor choice of distribution can simultaneously bias the fitted values toward an inappropriate shape and misweight observations relative to their true informativeness. This dual role is why actuaries examine residual diagnostics, mean-variance relationships in the raw data, and the natural range of the response before selecting a random component, rather than defaulting automatically to any single distribution regardless of context. Getting this choice right is foundational to producing a well calibrated, efficient rating model.
  27. The correct answer is B (The binomial distribution, commonly used for modeling probabilities and proportions): The logit natural parameter theta equal to log(mu over (1 minus mu)) together with the bell shaped variance function mu times (1 minus mu) are exactly the defining canonical link and variance function pair for the binomial distribution. Neither the normal, Poisson, nor gamma distribution has a bounded, bell shaped variance function of this specific form, since the normal has constant variance, the Poisson has variance equal to the mean, and the gamma has variance proportional to the mean squared. Recognizing this pairing quickly is a useful diagnostic skill when working backward from a described link and variance function to identify the underlying distribution.
  28. The correct answer is B (Because log(y!) depends only on the observed data y, which is identical across competing models): Since log(y!) is entirely a function of the observed response values and does not depend on the fitted mean mu or the regression coefficients at all, it remains exactly the same constant term regardless of which competing model, meaning which set of predictors or link function, is being fitted to the same underlying dataset. When comparing log-likelihoods or computing deviance differences between models fit to identical data, this term cancels out entirely and can safely be dropped from the computation. It still matters, however, when computing an absolute log-likelihood value or an information criterion like AIC that requires the full expression.
  29. The correct answer is C (A distribution belongs to the exponential family if its density can be rearranged into the standard exponential form): The defining test for exponential family membership is purely structural, whether the density or probability mass function can be manipulated through algebra into the form exp[(y*theta minus b(theta)) over a(phi), plus c(y,phi)], with theta the natural parameter and phi the dispersion parameter. This structural test does not require the mean to equal the variance, since only the Poisson happens to have that property among the common members, nor does it forbid a separate scale parameter, since the gamma and normal distributions both have one. Many, but not all, common distributions pass this test, which is precisely why some distributions like the lognormal, in its natural mean parameterization, fall outside the standard GLM framework.
  30. The correct answer is A (The fitted expected claim count is approximately 606.5): The linear predictor here is eta equal to 6.908 plus (negative 0.5), which equals 6.408, and exponentiating this full value under the log link gives the fitted mean mu equal to exp(6.408), which is approximately 606.5. Because the offset log(1000) has its coefficient fixed at exactly one by construction, exponentiating the full linear predictor automatically incorporates the exposure multiplicatively, here scaling the baseline rate down by the factor exp(negative 0.5), which is approximately 0.607, relative to the raw exposure of 1000. This calculation shows precisely how an offset combines with the remaining coefficients to produce a properly exposure-adjusted fitted count.
  31. The correct answer is A (The fitted mean severity is approximately 200.3, and exponentiating the coefficient gives a multiplicative rate relativity): Since the log link satisfies mu equal to exp(eta), substituting eta equal to 5.3 gives mu approximately equal to 200.3 as stated. On the log scale, a coefficient of 0.3 for a particular class means that class's linear predictor is 0.3 higher than the baseline, and exponentiating this coefficient, exp(0.3) approximately equal to 1.35, gives the multiplicative relativity by which the fitted mean severity for this class exceeds the baseline severity, exactly the multiplicative interpretation that makes the log link so useful for actuarial rate relativities. Actuaries routinely present rating factors this way so underwriters can quickly compare relativities across many rating variables.
  32. The correct answer is B (Keeping eta unbounded allows ordinary linear algebra techniques to be used for the systematic component): Separating the unrestricted linear predictor eta from the constrained fitted mean mu through the link function means the systematic component can be built using simple, additive, linear combinations of predictors and coefficients without needing to worry about accidentally violating a range restriction during that step. All the responsibility for mapping into a valid range for the response, such as strictly positive values or values between zero and one, is delegated entirely to the inverse link function applied afterward. This clean separation of responsibilities is a major reason the GLM framework remains both mathematically tractable and flexible enough to handle many different response types.
  33. The correct answer is D (Because theta is the parameter that enters linearly inside the exponent of the exponential family density): Because the density's exponent contains the term y*theta minus b(theta) with theta appearing linearly alongside y, differentiating the log-likelihood with respect to theta produces especially simple expressions involving y minus b'(theta), which directly connects to the mean through b'(theta) equal to mu. Working with mu directly instead would generally produce messier derivative expressions depending on the specific distribution. This mathematical convenience is exactly why the canonical link, defined as the function that sets theta equal to eta, produces the cleanest possible score equations among all valid link function choices.
  34. The correct answer is A (The statement is correct, and a non-canonical link may fit or interpret more naturally): Any sufficiently smooth, monotonic function that maps the valid range of mu onto the entire real line technically qualifies as a valid link function, and the canonical link is simply one particularly convenient choice among many, not the only mathematically permissible one. Choosing a non-canonical link, such as the log link for a gamma distribution instead of its canonical inverse link, can sometimes produce a better fitting or more interpretable model at the cost of losing the exact cancellation of variance and derivative terms that makes the canonical link's score equations especially simple. Actuaries routinely make this tradeoff deliberately, as with the widespread preference for the log link in gamma severity models.
  35. The correct answer is B (The framework allows the choice of distribution and link function to be matched to the true): Everything covered throughout this material, the exponential family form, the identification of the mean and variance from the cumulant function, the three GLM components, and the recognition that OLS is only the narrow normal, identity link special case, builds toward this single unifying benefit: actuaries can select a random component and link function that genuinely match the shape, range, and variance structure of frequency, severity, or probability data, rather than forcing every response into the restrictive assumptions that OLS silently imposes. This matching produces more efficient, better calibrated, and more sensible fitted models for the kinds of skewed, bounded, and heteroskedastic data that arise constantly in insurance ratemaking and reserving work. This benefit is precisely what makes the GLM framework the standard modeling approach across actuarial ratemaking practice.
  36. The correct answer is A (The deviance formula for a normal GLM with the identity link reduces exactly to the sum): The general deviance is defined as twice the difference between the log-likelihood of a saturated model, where each observation is fit perfectly, and the log-likelihood of the fitted model, and when this general formula is evaluated for the normal distribution under the identity link, it simplifies algebraically to exactly the sum of squared residuals familiar from OLS, up to the constant sigma squared. This confirms, alongside the earlier score equation result, that OLS is not merely analogous to a GLM but is precisely recovered as the identity link, normal random component special case even in its goodness of fit measure. For other distributions the deviance takes a different but analogous form, always reducing to the same saturated-versus-fitted comparison.
  37. The correct answer is C (The canonical link is defined as the function g such that g(mu) equals theta): By definition, the canonical link function for a given exponential family distribution is precisely the function that expresses the natural parameter theta as a function of the mean mu, so that when this same function is used as the GLM link, g(mu) equal to eta becomes theta equal to eta directly. This is exactly the property that produces the algebraic simplification in the score equations discussed earlier in this material. Each of the four common distributions covered here has its own specific canonical link determined entirely by its own particular b(theta) function and the corresponding theta-to-mu relationship.
  38. The correct answer is A (No, the exponential family structure of the random component is unaffected by the link choice): The random component and the link function are genuinely separate ingredients within the three-part GLM structure, so choosing the log link instead of the canonical inverse link for a gamma model changes only how the linear predictor eta relates to the fitted mean mu, while the underlying distribution assumed for the response, its density, its variance function, and its dispersion parameter, remain entirely gamma throughout. This independence between the random component and the link function is exactly what gives actuaries the freedom to mix and match link functions with distributions as practical interpretability considerations, such as the multiplicative relativities the log link provides, dictate. This flexibility is a routine part of how actuaries build and tune severity models in real rating work.
  39. The correct answer is D (Insurance claim data commonly violate the OLS assumptions of an unbounded response and constant variance): This statement ties together every theme developed throughout this material, the poor fit of OLS to non-negative, skewed, or heteroskedastic insurance responses, the unifying exponential family form that encompasses the normal, Poisson, gamma, and binomial distributions, the three-component GLM structure that separates the random component, systematic component, and link function, and the recognition that OLS survives within this larger framework only as its most restrictive special case. Understanding this motivation is essential context for why GLMs, rather than plain linear regression, became the standard actuarial tool for ratemaking and related predictive modeling tasks. Recognizing this motivation clarifies why the GLM framework, not OLS, became the actuarial standard for ratemaking work.
  40. The correct answer is B (Yes, because the log link is the canonical link for the Poisson distribution): Since the log link satisfies theta equal to log(mu) equal to eta exactly for the Poisson distribution, it is precisely the canonical link case, and the general result derived earlier, that canonical link score equations reduce to the sum over observations of (y minus mu) times x_j divided by a(phi), applies here with a(phi) equal to one by convention. This confirms the simplified score equation observed for this Poisson GLM is not a special coincidence but a direct instance of the general canonical link simplification that applies uniformly across every exponential family member whenever its own canonical link is chosen as the model's link function. This is exactly the kind of structural check an actuary should perform when reviewing any fitted GLM specification.
  41. The correct answer is D (Because the binomial likelihood factors identically whether written per policy or aggregated per class): Since each policyholder's renewal outcome is modeled as an independent Bernoulli trial sharing the same fitted probability mu within a rating class, the joint likelihood for all policyholders in that class factors into the binomial likelihood for the count of successes out of n_i trials, and maximizing this aggregated binomial likelihood produces exactly the same coefficient estimates as maximizing the product of individual Bernoulli likelihoods. This equivalence is a direct consequence of the exponential family structure and is why actuaries can freely choose whichever data representation, individual or grouped, is more convenient without affecting the resulting fitted model. This equivalence is a useful practical fact whenever raw individual-level data are unavailable but class-level totals are known.
  42. The correct answer is C (Because averaging more individual gamma distributed claims within a class reduces the variance of that class's): When several independent, identically distributed gamma claims are averaged together within a rating class, the variance of that average shrinks in inverse proportion to the number of claims averaged, exactly the statistical behavior captured by incorporating the claim count as a prior weight in the GLM variance formula, a(phi) equal to phi divided by the weight. This ensures that classes built from many claims, whose average severity is more precisely known, are appropriately given more influence during estimation than classes built from only a few claims. This weighting mechanism generalizes the same prior weight logic seen earlier for grouped binomial data.
  43. The correct answer is B (The link function maps the mean mu to the linear predictor eta): By definition g(mu) equals eta describes the link function's direction, taking the constrained mean and mapping it onto the unrestricted linear predictor scale, while the inverse link function g to the negative one power applied to eta recovers mu, the direction actually used to compute fitted values from a fitted model. For the log link, g(mu) equal to log(mu) is the link function while its inverse, exp(eta), is the inverse link that produces the fitted mean directly. Keeping these two directions straight is essential for correctly interpreting coefficients and computing fitted values from any GLM output.
  44. The correct answer is C (The odds of litigation decrease by a factor of approximately 0.82 for a one unit increase): A negative coefficient under the logit link means a one unit increase in the predictor decreases the log odds of litigation by 0.20, and exponentiating this coefficient, exp(negative 0.20) approximately equal to 0.82, gives the multiplicative factor by which the odds themselves change, here a decrease to about 82 percent of their previous value. This is the standard way actuaries interpret logistic regression coefficients on the more intuitive odds scale rather than the raw log odds scale that the model is actually estimated on. Reporting results this way helps non-technical stakeholders correctly interpret the practical impact of a fitted coefficient.
  45. The correct answer is B (Because GLM maximum likelihood estimation properly accounts for the true mean-variance relationship of the response): When the chosen random component correctly reflects how the true variance of the data depends on the mean, the resulting maximum likelihood estimates achieve the Cramer-Rao efficiency bound for that model, appropriately down-weighting noisier observations and up-weighting more precise ones through the variance function in the score equations. OLS, by contrast, assumes constant variance regardless of the mean, which is generally the wrong weighting scheme for frequency, severity, or probability data, leading to estimates that remain unbiased under mild conditions but are no longer the most efficient choice available. This efficiency gain is a central practical reason GLMs are preferred over OLS for actuarial ratemaking whenever the response deviates from the normal, constant variance assumption.

This exact balancing at the aggregate level is a well known and useful property of GLMs fit under their canonical link with an intercept, and it is one reason actuaries can trust that a fitted GLM will reproduce the overall observed total exactly even while distributing that total differently across rating classes. Understanding this property helps an actuary sanity check that a fitted GLM behaves as expected at the portfolio level.

This means observations with higher fitted means are, in relative terms, more precisely estimable, not less, even though their absolute variance in raw units is larger. Understanding this distinction between absolute and relative precision is important when interpreting how the GLM variance structure actually weights different observations during estimation.

This quadratic scaling of variance with the mean is precisely the structural feature that distinguishes the gamma distribution's mean-variance relationship from the linear scaling seen under the Poisson distribution.

This compounding is exactly why the Tweedie distribution, discussed earlier as a direct model for pure premium, arises naturally as a compound Poisson gamma process rather than as a simple product of two separately specified mean-variance relationships. Recognizing this compounding is essential when deciding whether to model pure premium directly or in two separate stages.

This demonstrates concretely how the prior weight, representing the number of trials underlying a grouped proportion, shrinks the variance of the resulting proportion response compared to the variance of a single ungrouped Bernoulli outcome.

Incorporating these known weights directly into the variance formula, rather than treating every row as equally informative, ensures the GLM correctly reflects that observations built from more underlying exposure carry more statistical information. This use of prior weights is a routine and important part of building actuarial GLMs on real aggregated insurance data.

Together they combine multiplicatively in the variance formula so that both the overall distributional scale and the observation-specific exposure level jointly determine the variance assumed for each row. Keeping this distinction clear is important when interpreting GLM output, since only phi is a fitted model output while the weights are supplied as known data inputs.

This misweighting can distort the fitted coefficients toward giving undue influence to small, noisy classes and can also produce standard errors and confidence intervals that misrepresent the model's true uncertainty. Including the correct prior weight, the claim count per class, restores the appropriate relative influence each observation should have during estimation.

This is precisely why choosing the wrong distribution, even while keeping the same predictors and even the same link function, can meaningfully change the fitted coefficients through this altered weighting, not merely through a different assumed shape for the fitted mean. This distinction is why actuaries pay close attention to distributional assumptions, not just to which predictors are included.

This distinction between quasi-likelihood and true likelihood based estimation is an important nuance for actuaries working with real, frequently overdispersed claim frequency data. Practitioners commonly favor this approach precisely because it needs no change to the coefficient estimation step itself.

An actuary who does not understand this underlying exponential family structure cannot correctly interpret whether a reported deviance value indicates a good or poor fit, since what counts as a reasonable deviance depends entirely on which distribution generated the underlying likelihood in the first place. Actuaries must therefore always report which distribution underlies a stated deviance value before it can be judged meaningful.

This same degrees of freedom adjustment generalizes to estimating phi for other distributions with a genuine free dispersion parameter, such as the gamma distribution, using the residual deviance in place of the sum of squared residuals. This adjustment mirrors the familiar degrees of freedom correction used throughout classical linear regression theory.

Recognizing this one general formula, rather than memorizing four unrelated variance rules, is what allows an actuary to understand GLM variance structure, weighting, overdispersion, and diagnostics as a single coherent topic rather than a collection of disconnected special cases. Internalizing this single formula is a foundational step toward mastering GLM diagnostics and model comparison more broadly.
