Comparing these two genuinely different specifications requires goodness of fit tools appropriate for non-nested models, such as comparing deviance relative to each model's own appropriate benchmark or using an information criterion like AIC, rather than a simple nested likelihood ratio test. Recognizing which comparisons are nested and which are not is an important practical skill when evaluating competing GLM specifications.

This conceptual bridge is exactly why introductory GLM material consistently develops the OLS special case explicitly before moving on to the more general and practically important non-normal cases actually used throughout actuarial rating work. This progression from OLS to the general GLM case is exactly how most introductory actuarial courses are structured.

This distinction between the raw log-scale coefficient and its exponentiated multiplicative effect is a common source of small interpretation errors that actuaries must be careful to avoid when communicating GLM results. Careful communication of this distinction matters most when relativities are being explained to non-technical audiences.

No regulatory mandate or universal optimality claim explains this dominance; rather it reflects a genuinely strong structural and practical fit between this specific combination of random component and link function and the actual behavior of insurance severity data. No single alternative combination matches this practical and structural fit as consistently across typical severity datasets.

This flexible, modular structure, unified by the shared exponential family mathematics and estimation machinery covered throughout this material, is exactly why the term generalized linear model refers to an entire class of models rather than any single specific one, including OLS itself as merely one narrow member of this much larger family. This modularity is precisely what gives the GLM framework its broad applicability across many different actuarial modeling tasks.

This calculation illustrates the constant coefficient of variation property of the gamma distribution discussed earlier in this material.

This property depends entirely on the choice of log link and would not occur under the identity link regardless of which random component, gamma, Poisson, or otherwise, is paired with it, confirming that the link function, not the random component, is responsible for this specific multiplicative behavior. This mathematical property is exactly why actuaries favor the log link whenever multiplicative relativities are the modeling goal.

This deliberate matching of distributional structure to the true nature of each response type, rather than any external mandate, is precisely the modeling discipline that the exponential family framework and the broader GLM structure exist to support throughout actuarial practice. Selecting the correctly matched distribution for each response type is therefore a foundational actuarial modeling skill.

This baseline fitted value represents the expected claim frequency for the reference class against which every other rating relativity in the model is multiplicatively compared once its own coefficient is exponentiated and applied. This baseline interpretation is a standard first step when explaining a fitted GLM's rating structure to stakeholders.

Every distribution and link combination discussed throughout this material, from the Poisson log link frequency model to the binomial logit link probability model, and including OLS itself as the normal identity link special case, is fully described once all three of these components have been specified explicitly. Every specific GLM an actuary ever builds is fully determined once these three components have been chosen explicitly.

This clean numeric relationship is exactly why actuaries favor odds ratios when communicating logistic regression results.

Internalizing this overarching structure, rather than treating each distribution or formula as an isolated fact, is the foundational goal of an introductory treatment of generalized linear models for actuarial practice. Mastering this overarching structure equips an actuary to apply GLMs confidently across frequency, severity, and probability modeling tasks.

Claim severity is bounded below by zero, so a negative prediction is nonsensical and signals a structural mismatch between the model and the data. A GLM with a log link keeps the fitted mean strictly positive by construction. This is one of the classic motivations for moving from OLS to a generalized linear model in insurance ratemaking.
  27. The correct answer is C (OLS assumes constant error variance across observations, violating the actual heteroscedastic pattern): Classical OLS is built on the homoscedasticity assumption, meaning every observation's error term is assumed to share one common variance regardless of the predicted mean. Insurance losses routinely show variance increasing with the mean, a pattern OLS has no mechanism to represent. Ignoring this mismatch produces inefficient estimates and misleading standard errors. A GLM instead lets the variance be an explicit function of the mean through the variance function V(mu).
  28. The correct answer is B (The symmetric normal error assumption poorly represents the true skewed distribution of outcomes): OLS implicitly treats deviations above and below the mean as equally likely and normally distributed, which is a poor description of loss data that piles up near zero with a long right tail of large claims. This mismatch leads to inefficient parameter estimates and unreliable prediction intervals. A GLM instead allows the analyst to choose a distribution, such as gamma or Poisson, that actually reflects the shape of the data. This flexibility is a core reason GLMs replaced OLS in most actuarial ratemaking work.
  29. The correct answer is B (OLS treats claim counts as continuous and can predict fractional or negative counts, unlike a Poisson GLM): Claim frequency is a discrete, non-negative count, but OLS has no way to restrict its fitted values to that support, so predictions such as negative counts or fractions of a claim are entirely possible. A Poisson GLM with a log link keeps predictions positive and reflects the discrete counting nature of claim frequency directly. It also correctly ties the variance to the mean rather than assuming a fixed variance for every policy. This alignment between distributional assumptions and the actual data generating process is why Poisson regression is standard for frequency modeling.
  30. The correct answer is B (A log link makes the linear predictor act multiplicatively on the original mean scale): Choosing a log link means the linear predictor is modeled on the log scale, so exponentiating it converts the additive combination of rating factors back into a product of individual relativities on the mean. This naturally produces the multiplicative rating structure actuaries use in practice, where each rating variable contributes a factor rather than a fixed dollar amount. OLS with an identity link cannot reproduce this multiplicative behavior directly. The choice of link function is therefore central to matching the GLM to how insurance rates are actually structured.
  31. The correct answer is C (The constant variance assumption underlying OLS standard errors is violated by the data): A funnel-shaped residual plot is the textbook signature of heteroscedasticity, meaning the spread of residuals changes systematically with the fitted mean rather than staying constant as OLS requires. When this assumption fails, the standard errors and hypothesis tests produced by OLS become unreliable even if the point estimates remain unbiased. A GLM addresses this directly by specifying a variance function V(mu) that lets the variance scale with the mean in a way consistent with the chosen distribution. This is one of the clearest diagnostic reasons actuaries move away from OLS toward GLMs.
  32. The correct answer is D (OLS treats pure premium as unbounded and normally distributed, ignoring the point mass at zero and the lower bound): The normal distribution underlying OLS places positive probability on all real numbers, including negative values, and cannot represent a spike of probability exactly at zero. Pure premium, by contrast, is bounded below by zero and often has many policies with no losses at all. Tweedie or compound Poisson-gamma GLMs are built specifically to accommodate this mixed discrete-continuous structure. OLS simply lacks the distributional flexibility to match this common actuarial data shape.
  33. The correct answer is C (A GLM lets the analyst match the response distribution and variance structure to the true nature of the data, which OLS cannot do): The essential advantage of a GLM over OLS is structural flexibility, since the analyst can choose a response distribution from the exponential family, such as Poisson, gamma, or binomial, and a variance function that actually reflects how the data behave. OLS forces a normal distribution with constant variance and an identity link regardless of whether that matches the underlying process. This mismatch in OLS leads to poor fit, unrealistic predictions, and unreliable inference for the kinds of skewed, bounded, and heteroscedastic data common in insurance. The GLM framework was developed specifically to overcome these limitations while retaining much of the interpretability of linear regression.
  34. Since the coefficient of variation is the standard deviation divided by the mean, and standard deviation is proportional to mu, this ratio stays constant across different mean levels. This matches the common empirical observation in severity data that relative variability does not shrink or grow systematically with claim size. OLS, by contrast, assumes a fixed absolute variance regardless of the mean, which cannot reproduce this behavior.
  35. The correct answer is C (The log link in the Poisson GLM exponentiates the linear predictor, which is always positive): With a log link, the fitted mean is obtained by exponentiating the linear predictor, and the exponential function is strictly positive for any real-valued input. This guarantees the Poisson GLM can never produce a negative predicted frequency, no matter how the linear predictor combines the rating variables. OLS with an identity link has no such safeguard, since a negative sum of coefficient effects maps directly to a negative fitted value. This structural difference is one of the practical reasons the log link is standard for frequency modeling.
  36. The correct answer is B (OLS can produce fitted probabilities outside the valid zero to one range): When the response is a binary indicator, its expected value is a probability, which must lie strictly between zero and one. OLS places no constraint on the fitted values of a linear predictor, so it can easily produce predictions below zero or above one, both of which are meaningless as probabilities. A binomial GLM with a logit link instead maps the linear predictor through the logistic function, which is mathematically guaranteed to stay within the zero to one interval. This is exactly why logistic regression, not OLS, is the standard tool for binary insurance outcomes such as renewal or lapse.
  37. The correct answer is D (the random component describing the distribution, the systematic component describing the linear predictor, and the link function connecting them): A generalized linear model is formally built from a random component that specifies the distribution of the response from the exponential family, a systematic component that combines the explanatory variables into a linear predictor, and a link function that connects the mean of the response to that linear predictor. Together these three pieces fully determine how the model translates predictor values into a predicted mean and how uncertainty around that mean is characterized. Changing any one of the three, for example swapping the distribution or the link, produces a genuinely different model. This three-part structure is what distinguishes GLMs from ordinary linear regression, which fixes the distribution as normal and the link as identity.
  38. The correct answer is D (the linear combination of explanatory variables, often written as eta equals X beta): The systematic component of a GLM is the linear predictor, typically denoted eta, formed by combining the explanatory variables and their coefficients in a linear fashion, exactly as in ordinary linear regression. It is called systematic because it captures the deterministic, structured part of the model that depends on the observed predictors. This linear predictor is not the mean of the response directly, since the link function is what connects eta to the mean mu. Separating the systematic component from the random component is what gives GLMs their flexibility to model non-normal, non-linear-in-mean relationships while keeping a linear structure in the predictors.
  39. The correct answer is B (it connects the mean of the response distribution to the linear predictor through a monotonic transformation): The link function g is defined so that g(mu) equals the linear predictor eta, providing a monotonic and typically invertible bridge between the natural scale of the mean and the unrestricted scale on which the linear predictor lives. This transformation is what allows a linear combination of predictors, which can take any real value, to map onto a mean that may be constrained, such as being strictly positive or bounded between zero and one. Different link functions produce genuinely different models even when the same distribution and predictors are used. The identity link, log link, and logit link are common examples, each suited to a different kind of response.
  40. The correct answer is B (They are genuinely different models because the link function changes how predictors relate to the mean): Although both models share the Poisson distribution, changing the link function changes the entire relationship between the predictors and the mean, so the two models are not interchangeable and produce different fitted values and coefficient interpretations. With an identity link the fitted mean can become negative for some predictor combinations, which is invalid for a Poisson mean that must stay non-negative, making the identity link a poor practical choice even though it remains mathematically defined for many predictor values. The log link avoids this problem by construction, guaranteeing a positive fitted mean. This illustrates why the choice of link, not just the choice of distribution, is a meaningful modeling decision.
  41. The correct answer is C (the assumed probability distribution of the response variable, drawn from the exponential family): The random component specifies the probability distribution assumed for the response given the predictors, and in the GLM framework this distribution must belong to the exponential family, which includes the normal, Poisson, gamma, and binomial distributions among others. This component determines both the shape of the response and, through the exponential family structure, the relationship between its mean and variance. Choosing the random component appropriately is what allows a GLM to represent counts, positive continuous amounts, or binary outcomes realistically, unlike OLS which fixes this choice to the normal distribution. The random component works together with the systematic component and the link function to complete the model specification.
  42. The correct answer is D (the natural or canonical parameter associated with the distribution): In the exponential family canonical form, theta is the natural parameter, and it is theta that carries the information linking the distribution to its mean through the cumulant function b(theta). The functions a(phi) and c(y,phi) handle the dispersion parameter and normalizing terms respectively, but theta specifically is the parameter that, when related to the linear predictor through the canonical link, gives the GLM its elegant mathematical properties. Different members of the exponential family, such as Poisson or gamma, correspond to different choices of b(theta) and different natural parameters. Understanding theta is essential to deriving both the mean and variance formulas that underlie GLM theory.
  43. The correct answer is C (taking the first derivative of b(theta) with respect to the natural parameter theta directly): A foundational result of exponential family theory is that the mean of the response equals b'(theta), the first derivative of the cumulant function with respect to the natural parameter theta. This relationship holds for every member of the exponential family and is what allows the mean function to be derived directly once b(theta) is known for a given distribution, such as exp(theta) for Poisson. The second derivative, b''(theta), similarly gives the variance function up to the dispersion parameter scaling. These derivative relationships are central to deriving canonical links and variance functions from first principles.
  44. The correct answer is C (a(phi) multiplied by the second derivative of b(theta), that is a(phi) times b''(theta)): The variance of a response from the exponential family equals a(phi) times b''(theta), where b''(theta) is the second derivative of the cumulant function with respect to the natural parameter, and a(phi) is a function of the dispersion parameter, often equal to phi itself for many common distributions. Since the mean is b'(theta), the second derivative b''(theta) captures how quickly the mean changes with theta, which turns out to directly govern the variance. This is the theoretical origin of the mean-variance relationship Var(Y) = phi times V(mu) that underlies practical GLM variance functions. Each exponential family member has its own b(theta), and therefore its own characteristic variance function V(mu).
  45. The correct answer is A (They can all be written in the common exponential family canonical form): Despite their differing shapes and supports, the normal, Poisson, gamma, and binomial distributions can each be expressed in the exponential family canonical form exp[(y*theta - b(theta))/a(phi) + c(y,phi)] with an appropriate choice of theta, b(theta), a(phi), and c(y,phi). This shared mathematical structure is precisely what allows a single unified estimation approach, based on maximum likelihood and iteratively reweighted least squares, to fit any of these distributions within the same GLM framework. It also means the general formulas for the mean, b'(theta), and variance, phi times b''(theta), apply uniformly across all of them. This unification is the theoretical foundation that makes GLMs a coherent generalization of ordinary linear regression rather than a loose collection of separate techniques.

This exponentiation step is why the log link automatically guarantees a positive fitted mean for any real valued linear predictor, an important property for count data. The log link is also the canonical link for the Poisson distribution, which gives it desirable statistical properties in estimation.

When the link function is chosen so that the linear predictor equals the natural parameter, this is called the canonical link, and for Poisson that canonical link is precisely the log link. Using the canonical link gives certain mathematical conveniences in estimation, including a particularly simple form for the score equations. This is why the log link is the standard default choice for Poisson frequency models in actuarial practice.

This means the natural parameter is proportional to the reciprocal of the mean, so the canonical link for the gamma distribution is the inverse link, g(mu) = 1/mu. This differs from the Poisson canonical link, reflecting the different mathematical structure of the gamma cumulant function. In practice actuaries often use a log link with gamma severity models instead of the canonical inverse link, because the log link gives the convenient multiplicative structure while the inverse link can be harder to interpret.

Squaring the mean gives 800 squared equals 640,000, and multiplying this by the dispersion parameter 0.15 gives 96,000. This property is a key reason the gamma distribution is a popular choice for modeling positive, right skewed severity data in actuarial work.

This constant coefficient of variation property is a defining characteristic of the gamma distribution's role in severity modeling.

The normal model instead forces every policy to share the exact same variance regardless of its predicted mean, which understates the uncertainty for high severity policies and overstates it for low severity ones. This mismatch is a core reason gamma GLMs, not OLS with a normal assumption, are the standard actuarial tool for severity modeling. Matching the variance function to the true data behavior improves both the efficiency of the parameter estimates and the realism of prediction intervals.

This framing is central to understanding why GLMs can handle insurance data that OLS cannot, while still reducing exactly to OLS as a special case when appropriate.

This function enters directly into the iteratively reweighted least squares algorithm used to fit GLMs, since observations are weighted inversely according to their assumed variance, giving more influence to precisely measured observations and less to noisier ones. Choosing a variance function that matches the true data behavior therefore improves both the efficiency of the parameter estimates and the accuracy of standard errors. This is fundamentally different from OLS, which always assumes a constant variance function regardless of the true relationship between mean and spread in the data.

As this power increases, the variance function becomes progressively more sensitive to changes in the fitted mean, so a small change in mu produces a much larger change in variance for inverse Gaussian than for normal. This ordering, often called the Tweedie power parameter family, helps actuaries select a distribution whose implied mean-variance sensitivity matches what is empirically observed in the data. Being able to select V(mu) appropriately lets the GLM more accurately reflect how uncertainty actually scales with predicted outcomes in real insurance data, improving both estimation efficiency and the realism of prediction intervals. The variance function V(mu), by contrast, is a fixed mathematical form determined entirely by which exponential family distribution is chosen, describing the shape of the dependence of variance on the mean, such as constant, linear, or quadratic in mu. Separating these two pieces allows the GLM framework to flexibly rescale the overall variance level through phi while still preserving the correct qualitative relationship between mean and variance through V(mu). Because deviance residuals, Pearson residuals, and related diagnostic tools all trace back to this same distributional structure, choosing a variance function that does not match the true data behavior can produce misleading residual patterns and unreliable goodness of fit assessments. This is why understanding V(mu) at the foundational level, as covered in this introductory GLM material, is a necessary prerequisite before interpreting more advanced diagnostic and model selection tools later in the syllabus. This mismatch can distort the fitted coefficients toward patterns driven by the noisier high mean observations and can also produce standard errors and confidence intervals that do not correctly reflect the true uncertainty in the estimates. Selecting a variance function that matches the empirical mean-variance relationship, for example by examining a plot of squared residuals against fitted values, is therefore an important practical step in GLM model building. This is one of the reasons actuaries compare multiple candidate distributions, such as Poisson, gamma, or Tweedie, when building a pricing model rather than defaulting automatically to any single choice.

Correctly matching distribution, link, and variance function to each named special case is a fundamental building block for recognizing how the broader GLM framework contains OLS, Poisson regression, gamma regression, and logistic regression all as particular instances of the same general theory.

By contrast, b(theta) is central to both the mean and variance formulas, and a(phi) appears directly in the variance formula, so those two functions cannot be dismissed as merely normalizing terms. Recognizing which piece of the canonical form is the nuisance term versus which pieces actively determine the mean and variance is a useful distinction for correctly deriving GLM properties from the general exponential family formula.

Keeping the link function inversion and the variance function application as two clearly separate steps helps avoid common calculation errors on exam problems of this type.

This illustrates that the canonical link, while theoretically elegant and computationally convenient in some respects, is not always the practically preferred choice, and actuaries frequently select a link function based on interpretability and real-world constraints rather than strict adherence to the canonical derivation. Both the canonical inverse link and the log link remain valid, estimable choices within standard GLM software, so the decision is a modeling judgment rather than a technical limitation.

GLMs instead allow the analyst to select from exponential family distributions such as Poisson, gamma, and binomial, each with its own variance function that appropriately ties variance to the mean, and to select a link function, such as log or logit, that respects the natural constraints of the response, such as non-negativity or boundedness between zero and one. This combination of distributional and structural flexibility is precisely why GLMs became the standard tool for actuarial ratemaking in place of ordinary least squares. Understanding this synthesis, rather than any single isolated fact, is the central learning objective of this introductory GLM chapter.

The correct answer is C (0.300, obtained by applying the inverse logit, exp(eta) divided by 1 plus exp(eta)): The inverse of the logit link is the logistic function, mu = exp(eta) / (1 + exp(eta)), and substituting eta = -0.847 gives exp(-0.847), which is approximately 0.4286, divided by 1.4286, giving a fitted probability of approximately 0.300. A negative linear predictor value correctly maps to a fitted probability below one half, since eta equal to exactly zero corresponds to a probability of exactly 0.500. This inverse transformation is essential for converting the model's internal linear predictor scale back into an interpretable probability that a claims adjuster or underwriter can use directly. Practicing this inversion in both directions, from probability to logit and from logit back to probability, is important preparation for interpreting logistic regression output on this exam.

Practice Test 27 Answer Key

  1. The correct answer is C (The general structure exp[(y*theta minus b(theta))/a(phi) plus c(y,phi)] applies to both probability mass functions and probability density functions, with c(y,phi) adjusting for the discrete or continuous nature of y): The exponential family canonical form is a general mathematical template that can represent both discrete probability mass functions, as with Poisson and binomial, and continuous probability density functions, as with normal and gamma, because the exponential structure itself does not require y to be either discrete or continuous, only that the resulting function correctly sums or integrates to one. The nuisance term c(y,phi) is what absorbs the distribution-specific normalizing details, including whether summation over integers or integration over a continuous range is required, while the theta and b(theta) portions carry the shared structure that produces the general mean and variance formulas covered earlier in this chapter. This is precisely why the same derivative-based formulas, mu equals b prime of theta and variance equals phi times b double prime of theta, apply uniformly regardless of whether the underlying distribution is discrete or continuous. This unification is one of the most elegant and practically useful features of exponential family theory as it applies to generalized linear models.
  2. The correct answer is A (The normal model assumes every policy shares the same variance regardless of its fitted mean, while the gamma model assumes variance grows with the square of each policy's fitted mean): The normal distribution's variance function is the constant V(mu) = 1, so under this model every policy is assumed to have the same variance regardless of how large or small its fitted mean severity happens to be, an assumption inherited directly from OLS. The gamma distribution's variance function is V(mu) = mu squared, so under this model policies with larger fitted mean severity are automatically assumed to have proportionally larger variance, specifically variance that scales with the square of the mean. Even though both models are fit to the exact same underlying data, the distributional assumption chosen by the analyst fundamentally changes what pattern of variance the model imposes on its predictions and standard errors. This comparison highlights concretely why the choice of random component in a GLM is not a cosmetic detail but a substantive modeling decision with real consequences for how the fitted model behaves.
  3. The correct answer is B (n adjusts the model's assumed precision to reflect that a proportion based on more underlying trials, such as more exposure units, is measured more precisely): When modeling a proportion, for example the fraction of claims within a group that were fraudulent, rather than a single binary indicator, the binomial GLM can incorporate the number of underlying trials n for each observation as a known weight, which effectively divides the variance by n, reflecting that a proportion computed from a larger number of trials carries less sampling variability than one computed from a small number of trials. This weighting is important in insurance applications where observations often represent aggregated groups of policies or exposures rather than individual binary outcomes, since treating every group's proportion as equally precise regardless of its underlying sample size would be statistically inappropriate. Correctly specifying these prior weights ensures the GLM appropriately downweights noisy, small-sample proportions relative to more reliable, large-sample proportions during estimation. This concept extends the basic exponential family framework introduced earlier to more realistic actuarial applications involving grouped or aggregated binomial data.
  4. The correct answer is A (First differentiate b(theta) once to obtain the mean function b prime of theta, then differentiate a second time and multiply by a(phi) to obtain the variance): The general procedure for any exponential family member is to differentiate the cumulant function b(theta) once with respect to theta to obtain the mean, mu equal to b prime of theta, and then differentiate a second time to obtain b double prime of theta, which when multiplied by a(phi) gives the variance, Var(Y) equal to a(phi) times b double prime of theta. This two-step differentiation procedure was applied consistently throughout this chapter to derive the mean and variance formulas for the Poisson, gamma, binomial, and normal distributions, each time starting from that distribution's specific cumulant function. Being able to state and apply this general procedure, rather than only memorizing the resulting formulas for each named distribution, is valuable exam preparation because it allows a candidate to correctly handle an unfamiliar or constructed cumulant function presented on an exam question. This procedure is one of the most fundamental theoretical results underlying the entire generalized linear model framework.
  5. The correct answer is B (the fitted mean is 1.00, since exp(0) equals 1, representing a baseline expected count of one claim): Applying the inverse of the log link, mu equal to exp(eta), and substituting eta equal to exactly zero gives mu equal to exp(0), which by definition equals 1. This shows that a linear predictor value of zero under a log link corresponds to a fitted mean of exactly one, not zero, which is an important distinction from what might be assumed by analogy to the identity link where a zero linear predictor would indeed produce a zero fitted mean. This baseline value of one often has a natural interpretation in a multiplicative rating structure, where the intercept term on the log scale, when exponentiated, represents the base expected frequency before any relativities from other rating variables are applied. Understanding this behavior of the log link at eta equal to zero is a useful conceptual check when interpreting GLM output or verifying a model's baseline predictions.
  6. The correct answer is A (A link function transforms the mean of the response on the model scale while the random variation is still modeled on the original scale, whereas transforming the response before OLS changes the scale on which the random variation itself is assumed to be normal and homoscedastic): In a GLM, the link function g relates the mean of the response, mu, to the linear predictor, so g(mu) equals eta, but the actual distribution assumed for the random component, including its variance function, is still specified on the original scale of the response y. By contrast, if an analyst instead transforms the response variable itself, for example by taking the log of severity before fitting OLS, the normal distribution and homoscedastic variance assumption underlying OLS are then applied on that transformed scale rather than the original scale, which changes the interpretation of residuals and can distort back-transformed predictions due to Jensen's inequality style bias. This distinction is subtle but important, since a log-linked Poisson or gamma GLM handles the mean transformation and the distributional assumption in a coherent, jointly estimated way, while a log-transform-then-OLS approach handles them somewhat inconsistently and requires an additional bias correction step when converting predictions back to the original scale. Recognizing this difference helps explain why GLMs are generally preferred over transform-then-OLS approaches in modern actuarial practice.
  7. The correct answer is D (the sample correlation matrix among all explanatory variables included in the model): The three components that formally define a generalized linear model are the random component, which specifies the exponential family distribution assumed for the response, the systematic component, which specifies the linear predictor formed from the explanatory variables, and the link function, which connects the mean of the response to that linear predictor. A sample correlation matrix among the explanatory variables may be a useful diagnostic tool for detecting multicollinearity before or after fitting a model, but it is not one of the three defining structural components of the GLM specification itself. Confusing a diagnostic tool with a structural model component is a common conceptual error, so distinguishing clearly between what defines the model and what is used to evaluate or diagnose the model is an important distinction for this exam. This question reinforces the same three-component definition introduced earlier in this chapter using a contrasting, deliberately incorrect fourth option.
  8. The correct answer is C (The gamma distribution respects the strictly positive support of claim amounts and better represents the heavier right tail associated with catastrophic claims): Claim severity data spanning from small routine claims to large catastrophic claims is a textbook example of a right skewed, strictly positive variable, which the gamma distribution is well suited to represent because of both its positive support and its variance function that scales with the square of the mean, naturally allowing more volatility for the larger claim categories. The normal distribution, by contrast, is symmetric and places positive probability on negative values, which is fundamentally inconsistent with claim amounts that can never be negative, and it also assumes constant variance regardless of claim size, understating the true volatility associated with catastrophic claims. Choosing the gamma distribution, typically paired with a log link, therefore produces a more realistic and better fitting model for this kind of heavy tailed severity data than a normal GLM or plain OLS regression would. This kind of reasoning about matching distributional shape and variance behavior to the actual characteristics of the data is exactly the practical skill this introductory GLM chapter aims to develop.
  9. The correct answer is A (b double prime of theta equals 1, since differentiating b prime of theta equal to theta with respect to theta gives exactly 1, confirming V(mu) equals 1): Starting from b(theta) = theta squared divided by 2, the first derivative is b'(theta) = theta, confirming the earlier result that the normal mean equals the natural parameter directly. Differentiating this result a second time, the derivative of theta with respect to theta is simply the constant 1, so b''(theta) = 1 for every value of theta. This confirms explicitly, through direct calculus rather than by assertion, that the normal distribution's variance function V(mu) is the constant 1, meaning the variance does not depend on the mean at all and equals the dispersion parameter phi alone. This explicit confirmation reinforces the earlier claim about the normal variance function and models the exact calculation technique a candidate should be prepared to reproduce for any cumulant function presented on the exam.
  10. The correct answer is A (OLS assumes a single continuous normal distribution across the entire response, which cannot represent both a discrete spike of probability at zero and a continuous skewed distribution for positive values simultaneously): Aggregate pure premium data for a policy is often modeled as a compound Poisson-gamma process, since a policy either has zero claims, giving a pure premium of exactly zero with meaningful probability, or has one or more claims, giving a continuous, right skewed positive pure premium. This mixed discrete-continuous structure cannot be represented by the single smooth, continuous, symmetric normal distribution that OLS assumes for its response, since OLS has no mechanism to place a distinct spike of probability exactly at zero separate from the continuous behavior for positive values. The Tweedie distribution, a special member of the exponential family with a power parameter strictly between 1 and 2, is specifically constructed to represent exactly this compound behavior within the standard GLM framework. This is one of the more advanced but practically important examples of why the exponential family and GLM framework, introduced in this chapter, offers capabilities that ordinary least squares simply cannot match for realistic insurance data.
  11. The correct answer is C (245, obtained correctly by exponentiating 5.5, the sum of the intercept and the territory coefficient): Under a log link, the model states log(mu) equals the linear predictor, so the fitted mean is recovered by exponentiating the full linear predictor, which here is the intercept 5.2 plus the coefficient 0.30 for a policy in the indicated territory, giving eta equal to 5.50. Exponentiating 5.50 gives approximately 244.7, which rounds to 245 dollars of fitted mean severity. This confirms the multiplicative interpretation of GLM coefficients under a log link, since exp(0.30) is approximately 1.35, meaning the territory indicator applies roughly a 35 percent upward relativity to the base severity of exp(5.2), approximately 181, and 181 times 1.35 also gives approximately 245. Correctly summing the full linear predictor before exponentiating, rather than exponentiating pieces separately and combining them incorrectly, is essential to this calculation.
  12. The correct answer is B (The likelihood function is built directly from the chosen distribution's probability density or mass function, so the estimating equations and iterative weighting scheme depend on which exponential family member is specified): Because each exponential family distribution has its own specific probability density or mass function, the log-likelihood used to fit a GLM via maximum likelihood is necessarily distribution-specific, and this in turn shapes the iteratively reweighted least squares algorithm commonly used to numerically maximize that likelihood. The weights applied at each iteration of this algorithm are directly tied to the variance function V(mu) of the chosen distribution, meaning a Poisson GLM, a gamma GLM, and a binomial GLM each follow a distinct sequence of weighted updates even when fit using the same general algorithmic approach. This is fundamentally different from OLS, where the closed form least squares solution does not require any iterative likelihood maximization at all under standard assumptions. Understanding that the exponential family distribution choice propagates all the way through to the mechanics of estimation reinforces why selecting an appropriate random component is a substantive rather than cosmetic modeling decision.
  13. The correct answer is A (Interpretability and alignment with real-world constraints, such as the multiplicative rating structure common in insurance, can outweigh the modest estimation convenience of the canonical link): Choosing the canonical link gives certain mathematical conveniences, including a simplified form for the score equations and guaranteed concavity of the log-likelihood under standard regularity conditions, but these conveniences are modest and modern GLM software handles non-canonical links with essentially the same reliability. Meanwhile a non-canonical choice such as the log link for a gamma severity model guarantees a strictly positive fitted mean and produces coefficients that combine multiplicatively, which matches how insurance rating factors are traditionally structured far better than the canonical inverse link does. Actuaries therefore routinely weigh practical interpretability and alignment with business needs against the comparatively small theoretical benefits of the canonical link, and in ratemaking practice the non-canonical log link wins out for gamma and often for other distributions as well. This illustrates that link function selection is ultimately a modeling judgment informed by both theory and practical context rather than a purely mechanical application of the canonical derivation.
  14. The correct answer is A (variance equals 6.00, standard deviation equals approximately 2.449, and coefficient of variation equals approximately 0.408): The true Poisson result uses variance equal to the mean directly, so variance equals 6.00, giving a standard deviation of the square root of 6.00, approximately 2.449, and a coefficient of variation of approximately 2.449 divided by 6.00, which equals approximately 0.408. A candidate who correctly recalls that Poisson variance always equals the mean, and who carefully performs the square root and division steps, arrives at this chain of calculations, while option C deliberately halves the true variance to test attentiveness. Notice that for Poisson data the coefficient of variation decreases as the mean increases, since the standard deviation grows only with the square root of the mean while the mean itself grows linearly, meaning relative variability shrinks for higher frequency risk classes. This declining coefficient of variation pattern is a useful conceptual takeaway distinguishing Poisson frequency behavior from the constant coefficient of variation pattern seen earlier for the gamma distribution.
  15. The correct answer is D (Because the shared canonical form exp[(y*theta minus b(theta))/a(phi) plus c(y,phi)] yields general, distribution-independent formulas for the mean and variance, allowing one unified theory to cover Poisson, gamma, binomial, normal, and other distributions used across different types of insurance data): The exponential family canonical form is foundational precisely because it is general enough to encompass a wide range of specific distributions, each obtained by choosing a particular b(theta), a(phi), and c(y,phi), while still yielding the same general derivative-based formulas for the mean, b prime of theta, and the variance, a(phi) times b double prime of theta. This generality is what allows a single body of GLM theory, including estimation via maximum likelihood, standard error calculation, and diagnostic tools like deviance residuals, to apply uniformly whether the actuary is modeling claim counts with Poisson, claim severity with gamma, binary outcomes with binomial, or continuous unbounded quantities with normal. Without this shared exponential family structure, actuaries would need an entirely separate and disconnected statistical theory for each distribution, making practical implementation and cross-model comparison far more difficult. This unifying role of the exponential family is the central conceptual thread running through every topic covered in this introductory GLM chapter.
  16. The correct answer is C (It supports using a Poisson GLM, since its variance function V(mu) equals mu directly, matching this observed proportional pattern, while OLS would impose a constant variance regardless of frequency level): When observed claim count variability scales up proportionally with the expected frequency, this matches the defining Poisson property that variance equals the mean, since the variance function is V(mu) = mu. An OLS model, by assuming constant variance for every policy regardless of its predicted frequency level, would systematically mismatch this pattern, understating uncertainty for high frequency classes and overstating it for low frequency classes. Selecting the Poisson GLM allows the fitted variance to automatically track the fitted mean in exactly the way the data actually behaves, improving both estimation efficiency and the realism of any resulting confidence intervals. This kind of diagnostic reasoning, comparing an observed mean-variance pattern against the known variance functions of candidate distributions, is a standard step in actuarial model selection.
  17. The correct answer is B (the natural log of lambda, since rearranging the mass function shows y times log(lambda) minus lambda appearing in the exponent): Taking the natural log of the Poisson mass function gives y times log(lambda) minus lambda minus log(y factorial), and comparing this to the canonical form y times theta minus b(theta), plus a term not involving theta, shows that theta must equal log(lambda) and b(theta) must equal lambda, which is exp(theta) once expressed in terms of theta. This derivation confirms from first principles, starting directly from the familiar Poisson probability formula, the same result used throughout this chapter that theta equals log(mu) for the Poisson distribution, since lambda is the Poisson mean. Being able to perform this rearrangement from the raw probability formula into canonical form is a valuable exam skill, since it does not rely on memorizing the canonical form in advance but instead derives it directly. This same rearrangement technique can be applied to the gamma, binomial, and normal probability formulas to independently verify each of their canonical forms.
  18. The correct answer is A (The normal distribution has a free variance parameter sigma squared that is not determined by its mean, so this variance enters as the dispersion parameter phi, whereas the Poisson variance is always fully determined by its mean with no separate free parameter): The normal distribution is characterized by two genuinely separate parameters, its mean and its variance sigma squared, and because the variance can take any positive value independent of the mean, it naturally enters the exponential family form as the dispersion parameter phi, which in this case equals sigma squared directly. The Poisson distribution, by contrast, has only a single parameter, lambda, which simultaneously determines both its mean and its variance, so there is no additional free variance parameter to estimate, and phi is conventionally fixed at exactly 1. This distinction explains why statistical software typically reports and estimates a separate dispersion or scale parameter for normal and gamma GLMs but not for standard Poisson or binomial GLMs. Recognizing which distributions have an estimable dispersion parameter and which have phi fixed by convention is an important practical detail when interpreting GLM output.
  19. The correct answer is D (A larger phi implies greater variance at any given fitted mean, since Var(Y) equals phi times V(mu) and V(mu) does not change based on phi): Because the general relationship is Var(Y) = phi times V(mu), and the variance function V(mu) is fixed by the choice of distribution rather than by phi, a larger estimated dispersion parameter directly scales up the implied variance at every fitted mean level, holding the distribution and mean fixed. This means two gamma GLMs with identical fitted means but different estimated phi values will imply different amounts of underlying variability in the severity data, with the larger phi model implying a noisier, more dispersed severity distribution. Since phi is typically estimated from the residual variation in the data rather than fixed by the distributional family for gamma and normal models, comparing phi across different model specifications or different subsets of data can be a useful diagnostic for how well a given rating structure explains the variability present in claim severity. This reinforces the earlier point that phi and V(mu) play distinct, multiplicative roles within the overall variance formula.
  20. The correct answer is A (The linear predictor eta is a linear combination of the coefficients and predictor values, but the link function then transforms eta nonlinearly to produce the fitted mean, so the relationship on the original response scale can appear nonlinear even though eta itself is linear in the predictors): The systematic component of a GLM, the linear predictor eta, is defined as a linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients, meaning it is linear in the parameters in exactly the same sense as ordinary linear regression. However, once a non-identity link function such as log or logit is applied to connect eta to the fitted mean mu, the relationship between the original predictors and mu on its natural scale becomes distinctly nonlinear, for example an exponential curve under a log link or an S-shaped curve under a logit link. This dual nature, linear in the coefficients on the eta scale but nonlinear in the fitted mean on the original scale, is exactly what gives GLMs the flexibility to model curved relationships while still retaining the estimation tractability of a linear model in the coefficients. Understanding this distinction is essential for correctly interpreting GLM coefficients, since a coefficient's effect on the fitted mean depends on the link function used, not simply on the coefficient's raw numeric value.
  21. The correct answer is B (the OLS model, since its identity link places no floor on the fitted mean and can produce a negative predicted claim count for an extreme combination of factors): Because OLS uses an identity link, the fitted mean is simply the raw linear combination of predictor effects, which places no mathematical restriction preventing the result from becoming negative when an unusual combination of rating factors happens to sum below zero, an outcome that is nonsensical for a claim count. The Poisson GLM's log link, by contrast, always exponentiates the linear predictor before producing the fitted mean, and the exponential function is strictly positive for any real input, so the Poisson GLM can never produce a negative predicted count regardless of how extreme the combination of predictor values becomes. This structural safeguard is one of the most practically important reasons actuaries prefer GLMs with an appropriate link function over OLS for policies at the edges of the rating variable space, where extreme combinations of factors are most likely to expose a model's structural weaknesses. Extreme or edge case policies are exactly where the theoretical differences between OLS and GLMs tend to become most visible in practice.
  22. The correct answer is C (0.600, obtained correctly by applying the inverse logit transformation, exp(0.405) divided by 1 plus exp(0.405)): Computing exp(0.405) gives approximately 1.499, and dividing this by 1 plus 1.499, or 2.499, gives approximately 0.600, so the fitted probability of attorney representation for this claim is approximately 60 percent. This calculation reverses the logit link by applying the logistic function directly to the linear predictor, which is the standard way to convert a fitted eta value from a binomial GLM back into an interpretable probability. Since eta is positive, the resulting probability correctly falls above one half, consistent with the general rule that a positive linear predictor under a logit link always corresponds to a fitted probability greater than 0.50. This calculation mirrors the inverse logit computations covered earlier in this chapter and reinforces the mechanical process of converting between the logit scale and the probability scale.
  23. The correct answer is D (It allows the assumed variance of each observation to change systematically with its own fitted mean, according to a distribution-specific function, rather than assuming every observation shares one identical fixed variance): The relationship Var(Y) = phi times V(mu) is the mechanism that ties each observation's assumed variance directly to its own fitted mean through the variance function V(mu), which differs by chosen distribution, for example equal to the mean for Poisson or proportional to the mean squared for gamma. Plain linear regression, by fixing the distribution as normal with V(mu) equal to the constant 1, structurally forces every observation to share the exact same variance regardless of its predicted mean, an assumption that is frequently violated by real insurance data. This single sentence captures the core statistical advantage of the GLM mean-variance framework over ordinary linear regression in a way that is independent of any one specific distribution. Being able to articulate this general principle concisely, separate from any particular numeric example, demonstrates a genuine conceptual grasp of why GLMs were developed as an extension of classical linear regression.
  24. The correct answer is D (8,874, obtained correctly by taking the square root of phi times mu squared, that is the square root of 78,750,000): First compute the variance using the gamma variance function, Var(Y) equals phi times mu squared, giving 0.35 times 15,000 squared, or 0.35 times 225,000,000, which equals 78,750,000. Taking the square root of 78,750,000 gives approximately 8,874, which is the standard deviation of severity implied by this fitted gamma model. Dividing this standard deviation by the mean gives a coefficient of variation of approximately 0.592, which also equals the square root of phi directly, since 0.35 has a square root of approximately 0.592, confirming the general property that a gamma GLM's coefficient of variation depends only on phi and not on the level of the fitted mean.
  25. The correct answer is B (Because writing the density in terms of theta produces the elegant derivative relationships mu equals b prime of theta and variance equals a(phi) times b double prime of theta, which do not hold as simply if the density is parameterized directly by mu): The natural parameter theta is called natural precisely because expressing the exponential family density in terms of theta, rather than directly in terms of the mean mu, produces the clean derivative-based relationships that connect the cumulant function b(theta) to both the mean and the variance of the distribution. This parameterization is what allows a single unified derivation, differentiate once for the mean and twice for the variance, to work identically across every exponential family member, from Poisson to gamma to binomial to normal. If the density were instead parameterized directly by mu, these convenient derivative relationships would generally not hold in the same simple form, and each distribution's mean and variance formulas would need to be derived by separate, distribution-specific methods. This mathematical convenience is why theta, not mu, is the parameter featured explicitly in the canonical exponential family form used throughout GLM theory.
  26. The correct answer is B (the random component first, specifying the distribution, followed by the systematic component, specifying the linear predictor, and finally the link function connecting them): While all three components ultimately work together and must be jointly specified before a GLM can be fit, a natural conceptual order for building up the model is to first decide on the random component, choosing which exponential family distribution best matches the nature of the response variable, then to specify the systematic component, deciding which explanatory variables and interactions enter the linear predictor, and finally to choose the link function that connects the fitted mean to that linear predictor in a way appropriate for the chosen distribution's support. This order reflects the typical actuarial workflow, where the analyst first examines the shape and support of the response data to select a distribution, then builds the rating structure through the linear predictor, and finally selects a link consistent with both choices. Although statistical software often requires all three to be specified together in a single model call, understanding this conceptual sequence helps clarify the distinct role each component plays in the overall model specification.
  27. The correct answer is A (The normal distribution assigns positive probability density to non-integer and negative values, neither of which can ever occur for an actual claim count, misrepresenting the true discrete, non-negative support of the data): Claim frequency is inherently a discrete count that can only take non-negative whole number values, but the normal distribution underlying OLS is defined continuously across the entire real number line, meaning it implicitly treats a claim count of negative one or 2.7 as having some, however small, positive probability, which is a fundamental mismatch with reality. The Poisson distribution, by contrast, is defined only on the non-negative integers, exactly matching the true support of a claim count variable, and a Poisson GLM with a log link further ensures the fitted mean itself stays strictly positive. This mismatch between the assumed continuous, unbounded normal distribution and the true discrete, non-negative nature of claim counts is one of the clearest and most intuitive reasons actuaries avoid OLS for frequency modeling in favor of a count-based GLM. Even when OLS produces seemingly reasonable point predictions on average, its underlying distributional assumption remains structurally inconsistent with the actual data generating process.
  28. The correct answer is B (0.100, obtained correctly by applying the inverse logit transformation to eta equal to -2.197): Applying the inverse logit formula, mu equals exp(eta) divided by 1 plus exp(eta), and substituting eta equal to -2.197 gives exp(-2.197), which is approximately 0.1111, divided by 1.1111, giving a fitted probability of approximately 0.100. This confirms that a negative linear predictor under a logit link correctly maps to a fitted probability below one half, consistent with this being a low risk policy with only about a 10 percent chance of at least one claim. This calculation reinforces the general pattern that as eta moves further into negative territory, the fitted probability under a logit link moves progressively closer to zero, while as eta moves further positive, the fitted probability moves progressively closer to one, always remaining strictly within the valid zero to one range.
  29. The correct answer is A (Deviance is defined based on the log-likelihood of the specified distribution, and since each exponential family member has its own distinct likelihood function, the resulting deviance formula is necessarily distribution specific): Deviance in a GLM is constructed as twice the difference between the log-likelihood of a saturated model, one that fits each observation perfectly, and the log-likelihood of the fitted model, and because the log-likelihood itself is built directly from the specific exponential family density assumed for the response, the resulting deviance formula necessarily differs across distributions. For a normal GLM with an identity link, this deviance formula reduces exactly to the residual sum of squares familiar from OLS, but for a Poisson, gamma, or binomial GLM the deviance formula takes on a different, distribution-appropriate mathematical form. This distribution dependence is precisely why deviance, rather than a fixed universal sum of squared residuals, is the standard goodness of fit measure used across the whole GLM framework, since it correctly generalizes the OLS residual sum of squares concept to any exponential family member. Understanding that deviance is fundamentally likelihood-based, and therefore distribution specific, is an important conceptual bridge between the exponential family theory covered in this chapter and later diagnostic topics in the GLM syllabus.
  30. The correct answer is D (Because V(mu) equals mu squared, risk classes with a higher expected severity, such as those prone to catastrophic fire losses, are automatically assigned a proportionally much larger variance, reflecting their greater potential for extreme outcomes): Since the gamma variance function is V(mu) equal to mu squared, a risk class with a substantially higher expected severity, such as one prone to occasional catastrophic fire losses, automatically receives a variance that scales with the square of that higher mean, correctly reflecting greater potential dispersion and the possibility of extreme large losses relative to lower severity risk classes. This quadratic scaling is what allows the gamma distribution to represent the coefficient of variation staying roughly constant across risk classes of very different average severity, a pattern commonly observed in actual claims data across many lines of business. A constant variance model, such as OLS with a normal assumption, would instead assign the identical variance to both a low severity risk class and a catastrophic fire prone risk class, badly understating the true volatility associated with the higher severity class. This direct link between the variance function's mathematical form and the real world pattern of increasing volatility with increasing severity is central to why the gamma distribution is standard for this type of insurance modeling.
  31. The correct answer is A (The log link, because theta equals log(mu) follows directly from inverting the Poisson mean relationship mu equals exp(theta)): The Poisson cumulant function b(theta) equal to exp(theta) produces the mean relationship mu equal to b prime of theta, which is also exp(theta), and inverting this to solve for theta in terms of mu gives theta equal to log(mu). Because the canonical link is defined as the function that sets the natural parameter theta directly equal to the linear predictor, and here theta equals log(mu), the canonical link for the Poisson distribution is confirmed to be the log link. This derivation, worked through algebraically rather than simply recalled from memory, demonstrates the general method for finding any distribution's canonical link, namely differentiate the cumulant function to get the mean, then invert that relationship to express theta as a function of mu. This same method was applied earlier in this chapter to derive the inverse link for gamma and the logit link for binomial, confirming the consistency of the underlying theoretical approach across different exponential family members.
  32. The correct answer is C (960,000,000, obtained correctly as phi times mu squared, that is 0.60 times 1,600,000,000): Squaring the mean of 40,000 gives 1,600,000,000, since 40,000 times 40,000 equals 1,600,000,000, and multiplying this by the dispersion parameter of 0.60 gives a variance of 960,000,000. Taking the square root of this variance gives a standard deviation of approximately 30,984, which divided by the mean of 40,000 gives a coefficient of variation of approximately 0.775, matching the square root of phi as expected for a gamma distribution. This large variance relative to the mean illustrates why commercial liability severity, often driven by a relatively high dispersion parameter reflecting substantial claim-to-claim variability, is considered a higher volatility line of business compared to lines with more homogeneous claim sizes. This calculation follows the identical two-step process, square the mean and multiply by phi, used consistently throughout this chapter for gamma variance calculations.
  33. The correct answer is A (V(mu) is a fixed function determined entirely by the chosen exponential family distribution, describing how variance depends functionally on the mean, while phi is typically a single scale parameter, sometimes fixed by convention and sometimes estimated from the data, that adjusts the overall magnitude of the variance): The variance function V(mu) is a mathematical form uniquely determined by which exponential family distribution has been selected as the random component, for example constant for normal, equal to mu for Poisson, or equal to mu squared for gamma, and it describes the qualitative shape of how variance changes as the mean changes. The dispersion parameter phi, by contrast, is typically a single overall scale factor, fixed at exactly 1 by convention for Poisson and binomial models, but estimated separately from the residual variation in the data for normal, gamma, and inverse Gaussian models. Together these two pieces multiply to give the full variance formula, with V(mu) supplying the functional shape and phi supplying the overall scale, and correctly distinguishing between these two roles is essential for interpreting GLM variance output correctly. Confusing the two, for example assuming phi changes the shape of the mean-variance relationship rather than only its overall scale, is a common conceptual error worth avoiding on this exam.
  34. The correct answer is B (Var(Y) equals phi times 1, which simplifies to phi, since b double prime of theta equals the constant 1 for this cumulant function): Differentiating b(theta) equal to theta squared divided by 2 twice gives b double prime of theta equal to the constant 1, as shown earlier in this chapter, so applying the general variance formula Var(Y) equals a(phi) times b double prime of theta with a(phi) equal to phi directly gives Var(Y) equals phi times 1, which simplifies to just phi. This confirms explicitly, through the exponential family derivation rather than by assertion, that the normal distribution's variance does not depend on mu at all and is instead governed entirely by the dispersion parameter phi, which for OLS is simply the constant error variance sigma squared. This result is exactly the constant variance assumption, homoscedasticity, that underlies classical OLS regression, now shown to emerge naturally as a special case of the general GLM variance formula. Seeing this derivation makes explicit why OLS occupies such a restrictive corner of the broader GLM framework.
  35. The correct answer is D (Because a normal distribution paired with an identity link produces exactly the same likelihood, estimating equations, and fitted coefficients as classical least squares regression, making OLS mathematically identical to this particular GLM specification rather than merely similar to it): Since the normal distribution can be written in exponential family canonical form with b(theta) equal to theta squared divided by 2, and its canonical link is the identity link as derived earlier, specifying a GLM with exactly this distribution and link reproduces the identical log-likelihood function that underlies classical OLS estimation. Maximizing this log-likelihood produces estimating equations that are algebraically identical to the normal equations solved directly in least squares regression, meaning the resulting fitted coefficients from the two approaches coincide exactly, not merely approximately. This precise equivalence, rather than a loose similarity, is what justifies calling OLS a true special case nested within the broader GLM framework instead of a separate technique that merely resembles a GLM. Recognizing this exact mathematical equivalence is the clearest possible demonstration that GLMs are a genuine generalization of, rather than a replacement for, ordinary least squares regression.
  36. The correct answer is D (approximately 3.00 claims, obtained by exponentiating 1.099, representing an above average frequency relative to the baseline of one): Applying the inverse of the log link, mu equal to exp(eta), and substituting eta equal to 1.099 gives exp(1.099), which computes to approximately 3.00. Since a linear predictor of exactly zero corresponds to a fitted mean of exp(0) equal to 1, as established earlier in this chapter, a positive linear predictor of 1.099 correctly maps to a fitted mean well above that baseline of one claim, confirming this policy has an above average expected frequency. This comparison against the eta equal to zero baseline is a useful conceptual anchor for interpreting whether any given fitted linear predictor represents a higher or lower than typical expected frequency under a log link. The relationship between eta and mu here again demonstrates the exponential, multiplicative nature of predictions under a log-linked Poisson GLM.
  37. The correct answer is D (The gamma GLM, since its variance function automatically assigns a proportionally larger variance to the high value home segment given its much larger fitted mean severity): Because the gamma variance function is V(mu) equal to mu squared, a high value home segment with a substantially larger fitted mean severity automatically receives a correspondingly larger variance under the gamma GLM, correctly reflecting the greater dollar volatility typically observed among more expensive homes. OLS, by assuming a single constant variance for every policy regardless of segment, would instead apply the same absolute variance to both modest and high value homes, understating the true uncertainty associated with the higher value segment and potentially producing overconfident premium estimates for that group. This example again demonstrates the practical, not merely theoretical, importance of matching the variance function to the actual behavior of insurance data, since an inappropriate variance assumption can directly translate into mispriced risk for specific segments of the book. Selecting an appropriate GLM distribution is therefore a core actuarial pricing decision, not just a statistical technicality.
  38. The correct answer is B (Since the mean itself is b prime of theta, a b(theta) whose second derivative grows quickly as theta increases corresponds to a variance that increases quickly as the mean increases, because both the mean and the variance move together as functions of the same underlying theta): Because the mean mu equals b prime of theta and the variance is proportional to b double prime of theta, both quantities are functions of the same underlying natural parameter theta, so as theta increases, both the mean and, if b double prime of theta is itself increasing, the variance increase together. A cumulant function whose second derivative grows quickly as theta increases, such as the gamma or inverse Gaussian cumulant functions compared to the Poisson cumulant function, therefore produces a variance function V(mu) that increases more sharply as a function of the mean itself. This is exactly the underlying mathematical reason that gamma and inverse Gaussian variance functions, mu squared and mu cubed respectively, grow faster with the mean than the Poisson variance function, which grows only linearly with the mean. Understanding this connection between the curvature of b(theta) and the resulting steepness of V(mu) as a function of mu provides a deeper theoretical grounding for the variance function comparisons made throughout this chapter.
  39. The correct answer is C (the two claims have exactly the same variance of 0.0475 each, since mu(1-mu) is symmetric around 0.5 and 0.05 and 0.95 are equally distant from that midpoint): Computing mu(1-mu) for the first claim gives 0.05 times 0.95, which equals 0.0475, and computing the same expression for the second claim gives 0.95 times 0.05, which is also 0.0475, since multiplication is commutative and 0.05 and 0.95 are simply the two factors in reversed order. This confirms that the binomial variance function mu(1-mu) is symmetric around mu equal to 0.5, meaning any two mean values equally distant from 0.5, in either direction, produce identical implied variances. Both claims here represent near-certain outcomes, one very unlikely to be denied and one very likely to be denied, and both carry correspondingly low variance since near-certain outcomes have little remaining uncertainty regardless of which direction that certainty points. This symmetry property is a useful quick mental check when working with binomial variance calculations on this exam.
  40. The correct answer is D (The underlying systematic component structure, a linear combination of explanatory variables forming the linear predictor eta, and the general derivative-based mean and variance relationships from exponential family theory, remain conceptually the same across all three named models, even though the specific distribution and link differ): Poisson regression, gamma regression, and logistic regression each use a genuinely different random component and link function, so their specific variance functions and link functions are not identical across the three, and their fitted numerical coefficients will naturally differ depending on the data and problem at hand. What remains constant is the underlying conceptual machinery, namely that each model builds a linear predictor eta from a linear combination of explanatory variables, and each model's mean and variance are derived from the same general exponential family relationships, mu equals b prime of theta and variance equals a(phi) times b double prime of theta, applied to that model's own specific cumulant function. This shared conceptual structure is exactly what makes it correct to describe all three models as members of one unified GLM framework rather than as three unrelated statistical techniques that happen to share a name. Recognizing what is shared at the structural level, versus what differs at the specific distributional level, is a key synthesis point for this introductory GLM chapter.
