The correct answer is B (2,000, obtained correctly by exponentiating the linear predictor, exp(7.601)): Because the log link satisfies log(mu) equal to eta, recovering the fitted mean requires exponentiating the linear predictor, so mu equals exp(7.601), which computes to approximately 2,000. This large fitted severity is consistent with a specialty liability line, which typically carries a higher average claim size than more routine personal lines coverage. As with every other log-link calculation in this chapter, the key step is exponentiating the full linear predictor rather than attempting any other transformation, since only exponentiation correctly reverses the log link relationship.
  42. The correct answer is C (The random component distribution changes from normal to Poisson, the variance function changes from constant to equal to the mean, and the link function changes from identity to log, while the systematic component, the linear combination of the same explanatory variables, stays structurally the same): Moving from a normal-identity GLM to a Poisson-log GLM changes two of the three defining GLM components, the random component and the link function, while the systematic component, meaning which explanatory variables enter the linear predictor and how they combine linearly, can remain exactly the same if the analyst chooses to keep it unchanged. The variance function correspondingly changes from the constant V(mu) equal to 1 under normal to V(mu) equal to mu under Poisson, since the variance function is a direct consequence of the chosen distribution. This clean separation, where the systematic component can be held fixed while the random component and link function are changed independently, illustrates the modular nature of the three-part GLM specification. Being able to precisely identify which of the three components changes and which stays fixed in any given model comparison is a useful skill for this exam.
  43. The correct answer is A (The word generalized refers to generalizing the random component beyond the normal distribution to any exponential family distribution, and generalizing the relationship between the mean and the linear predictor beyond the identity link to any suitable link function, while retaining the linear structure of the predictors themselves): The term generalized linear model captures precisely the two dimensions along which this framework extends ordinary linear regression, namely allowing the random component to be any distribution from the exponential family rather than only the normal distribution, and allowing the connection between the mean and the linear predictor to be any appropriate link function rather than only the identity link. The word linear in the name is retained because the systematic component, the way explanatory variables combine to form the linear predictor eta, remains a linear combination of coefficients and predictor values in every GLM, exactly as in ordinary linear regression. This precise naming reflects the actual mathematical structure of the model, generalized in its distributional and link function choices, but still linear in its systematic component, which is why understanding all three components, random, systematic, and link, together is essential to correctly understanding what a GLM is and is not. This naming convention distinguishes GLMs from fully nonlinear models, which relax the linearity of the systematic component itself rather than only the distribution and link.
  44. The correct answer is B (Because deviance is defined using each distribution's own log-likelihood, and the Poisson and gamma log-likelihoods differ from the normal one): Deviance is in fact defined generally using twice the difference in log-likelihood between a saturated model and the fitted model, and because the normal, Poisson, and gamma distributions each have distinct log-likelihood functions built from their own distinct probability density or mass functions, their resulting deviance formulas are correspondingly distinct rather than identical. The residual sum of squares formula familiar from OLS is simply the specific form that this general deviance definition happens to take when the normal distribution is the assumed random component, and it does not automatically transfer to other distributions. For a Poisson GLM the deviance formula instead involves logarithmic terms reflecting the Poisson log-likelihood, and for a gamma GLM it involves a different combination of logarithmic and ratio terms reflecting the gamma log-likelihood. Recognizing that deviance is fundamentally distribution specific, built from each distribution's own likelihood rather than from one universal formula, is an important conceptual foundation for later GLM diagnostic topics.
  45. The correct answer is D (approximately 0.671, obtained correctly since the coefficient of variation for a gamma distribution equals the square root of phi, and the square root of 0.45 is approximately 0.671): For a gamma distribution, the variance is phi times mu squared, so the standard deviation is the square root of phi times mu, and dividing this standard deviation by the mean gives the coefficient of variation equal to the square root of phi alone, independent of the actual mean value of 2,500. Computing the square root of 0.45 gives approximately 0.671, confirming that this class has a relative variability of roughly 67 percent of its mean severity regardless of what that mean happens to be. This property, that the gamma coefficient of variation depends only on phi and never on mu, was established earlier in this chapter and is reconfirmed here numerically, reinforcing why the gamma distribution is well suited to severity data whose relative, rather than absolute, variability tends to stay roughly constant across different average claim sizes.

Practice Test 28 Answer Key

  1. The correct answer is A (the normal distribution, whose variance function V(mu) equals the constant 1, so its variance is governed entirely by the dispersion parameter phi regardless of the mean): Among the Poisson, gamma, binomial, and normal distributions covered in this chapter, only the normal distribution has a variance function that is a constant, V(mu) equal to 1, meaning its variance under the general formula Var(Y) equals phi times V(mu) reduces simply to phi and does not vary at all with the fitted mean. The Poisson, gamma, and binomial distributions all have variance functions that genuinely depend on mu, namely mu itself, mu squared, and mu(1-mu) respectively, meaning their implied variance changes as the fitted mean changes across different observations. This constant variance property of the normal distribution is exactly the homoscedasticity assumption inherited by OLS regression, and it is precisely this lack of mean dependence that makes the normal distribution, and therefore OLS, a poor structural match for most insurance data, where variance is empirically observed to change systematically with the mean.
  2. The correct answer is B (Because deriving the mean and variance from first principles allows a candidate to correctly handle an unfamiliar or constructed cumulant function that does not correspond to any of the standard named distributions, rather than being limited only to distributions seen before): While memorizing the specific mean and variance formulas for Poisson, gamma, binomial, and normal distributions is useful and efficient for routine problems, genuinely understanding the underlying derivative-based derivation, differentiate the cumulant function once for the mean and twice for the variance, equips a candidate to correctly handle a novel or constructed cumulant function that may appear on an exam question without a directly memorized formula to fall back on. Several questions throughout this chapter deliberately used unfamiliar cumulant functions, such as b(theta) equal to theta cubed divided by 3, precisely to test whether a candidate can apply the general derivation method rather than only recall memorized results. This derivation-based understanding also builds a more robust foundation for later GLM topics, including deviance and model diagnostics, which themselves depend on the same underlying exponential family structure. Prioritizing understanding of the general method over memorization of specific formulas is therefore sound exam preparation strategy for this material.
  3. The correct answer is B (the inverse Gaussian distribution, since its variance function V(mu) equals mu cubed, which grows faster than the gamma distribution's V(mu) equal to mu squared as the mean increases): Comparing the two variance functions directly, the gamma distribution's V(mu) equal to mu squared grows with the second power of the mean, while the inverse Gaussian distribution's V(mu) equal to mu cubed grows with the third power, meaning that for sufficiently large mean values the inverse Gaussian variance function increases more rapidly than the gamma variance function. This makes the inverse Gaussian distribution an even more aggressive choice than gamma for representing severity data with an especially heavy right tail, where large claims carry disproportionately large uncertainty relative to their already large expected value. An actuary choosing between these two candidate distributions for a specific line of business would typically examine the empirical relationship between observed variance and mean in the actual claims data to decide which power relationship, mu squared or mu cubed, better matches reality. This comparison illustrates the broader Tweedie power parameter framework covered earlier in this chapter, where different power values of mu in the variance function correspond to different named distributions along a continuous spectrum.
  4. The correct answer is A (a gamma distribution paired with an identity link, since gamma requires a positive mean but identity allows zero or negative values): The gamma distribution is defined only for strictly positive values, meaning its mean must always be positive, but the identity link places no mathematical restriction preventing the linear predictor, and therefore the fitted mean under an identity link, from equaling zero or becoming negative for some combination of predictor values. This mismatch can cause the gamma likelihood to become undefined during the iterative fitting process whenever the algorithm explores a region of predictor space producing a non-positive fitted mean, leading to convergence failures or unstable estimates. By contrast, the other three combinations listed, Poisson with log link, binomial with logit link, and normal with identity link, are all internally consistent, since each link function's range matches the valid support of the corresponding distribution's mean. This example illustrates why actuaries must consider not just distributional shape but also the compatibility between the chosen link function's range and the chosen distribution's valid mean support when specifying a GLM.
  5. The correct answer is D (60, obtained correctly by exponentiating the full linear predictor, 4.0 plus 0.20 minus 0.10, which equals 4.10): The full linear predictor for this policy combines the intercept and both applicable coefficients, giving 4.0 plus 0.20 minus 0.10, which sums to exactly 4.10. Exponentiating this complete linear predictor, exp(4.10), gives approximately 60.3, which rounds to 60 dollars of fitted mean severity. This calculation reinforces that under a log link, every applicable coefficient, whether representing an increase such as the territory factor or a decrease such as the claims-free discount, must first be summed together with the intercept into the complete linear predictor before exponentiating, rather than being exponentiated separately and combined afterward, which would produce an incorrect result.
  6. The correct answer is A (OLS places no restriction guaranteeing the fitted mean stays between 0 and 1, while the logit link mathematically guarantees this by construction): A proportion, such as the fraction of a batch of 50 claims that were denied, is naturally bounded between 0 and 1, but OLS with its identity link places no mathematical constraint ensuring fitted values respect this boundary, meaning it can produce a nonsensical predicted proportion below 0 or above 1 for some combinations of predictors. A binomial GLM with a logit link, by contrast, always maps the linear predictor through the logistic function, which by its mathematical construction can only ever produce values strictly between 0 and 1, guaranteeing valid fitted proportions regardless of the predictor values involved. The binomial distribution can indeed be applied to grouped proportion data such as this, using the number of trials, here 50, as a prior weight that appropriately scales the assumed precision of each batch's proportion, exactly as discussed earlier in this chapter regarding binomial prior weights. This bounded-response scenario is another concrete illustration of why GLMs with an appropriately chosen link function structurally outperform OLS for many types of insurance data beyond just counts and severities.
  7. The correct answer is A (The canonical link is the specific link function obtained by setting the natural parameter theta directly equal to the linear predictor, which yields particular estimation conveniences, while a non-canonical link is still mathematically valid but does not share this exact algebraic identification between theta and the linear predictor): The canonical link is defined precisely as the link function that arises from setting the natural parameter theta equal to the linear predictor eta and then solving for theta as a function of mu, which for each of the four distributions covered in this chapter gives log for Poisson, inverse for gamma, logit for binomial, and identity for normal. This particular choice yields certain mathematical conveniences during estimation, but a non-canonical link, such as the log link commonly used with gamma instead of its canonical inverse link, remains a fully valid and often practically preferable choice, simply without that exact algebraic identification between theta and eta. Understanding this precise technical definition, rather than treating canonical as simply meaning best or only valid, clarifies why actuaries can and often do choose non-canonical links deliberately based on interpretability and practical constraints, as discussed earlier in this chapter regarding the gamma distribution's log link. This final synthesis question draws together the canonical link derivations performed for each of the four core distributions throughout this chapter.
  8. The correct answer is C (p equal to 0 corresponds to normal, p equal to 1 corresponds to Poisson, p equal to 2 corresponds to gamma, and p equal to 3 corresponds to inverse Gaussian): The Tweedie family variance function V(mu) equal to mu raised to the power p recovers each of the four core distributions covered in this chapter at specific integer values of p, namely p equal to 0 giving the constant variance function of the normal distribution, p equal to 1 giving the Poisson distribution's variance equal to the mean, p equal to 2 giving the gamma distribution's variance equal to the mean squared, and p equal to 3 giving the inverse Gaussian distribution's variance equal to the mean cubed. This ordering, increasing from 0 to 3, exactly matches the ordering of increasing sensitivity of variance to the mean discussed earlier in this chapter, with normal being least sensitive and inverse Gaussian being most sensitive among these four named distributions. Memorizing this specific correspondence between Tweedie power values and named distributions is a useful and efficient way to organize the variance function material covered across this entire chapter into one unified numerical framework. Values of p strictly between 1 and 2 correspond to the compound Poisson-gamma Tweedie distribution, which does not match any single one of the four named distributions but instead represents a genuinely distinct hybrid case useful for aggregate pure premium modeling.
  9. The correct answer is D (b prime of theta equals -1/theta, confirming the mean formula, and b double prime of theta equals 1/theta squared, which after substituting theta = -1/mu gives V(mu) equal to mu squared, confirming the gamma variance function): Differentiating b(theta) = -log(-theta) using the chain rule, with u equal to -theta, gives b'(theta) equal to -1/theta, which directly confirms the claimed mean formula mu equal to -1/theta stated in the question. Differentiating a second time, treating b'(theta) as -theta to the power negative 1, gives b''(theta) equal to theta to the power negative 2, or 1/theta squared, and substituting the inverted relationship theta equal to -1/mu into this expression gives 1 divided by (-1/mu) squared, which simplifies to mu squared. This confirms both the mean and variance formulas for the gamma distribution directly from its cumulant function through explicit differentiation, exactly reproducing the results stated without proof earlier in this chapter. Working through this full derivation demonstrates the complete mechanical process, differentiate twice and substitute the inverted mean relationship, that underlies every variance function derivation covered in this chapter.

Marine cargo claim severity, like most insurance severity data, is strictly positive and right skewed, characteristics the gamma distribution represents naturally while the symmetric, unbounded normal distribution underlying OLS does not. While a small sample size of 40 observations does raise separate concerns about the precision of any fitted model's coefficients, those concerns apply to both OLS and the gamma GLM equally and do not change which distributional assumption better represents the data's true shape. This distinction between distributional appropriateness and sample size adequacy is an important one for an actuary to keep separate when justifying a modeling choice to a colleague or regulator.

These two components work together with the link function, which connects the mean implied by the random component's distribution to the systematic component's linear predictor, to fully specify a GLM. Clearly separating what is deterministic, the systematic component, from what is random, the random component, is fundamental to understanding how a GLM produces both a point prediction and a corresponding measure of predictive uncertainty for any given policy. This distinction was reinforced repeatedly throughout this chapter using the Poisson, gamma, binomial, and normal distributions as concrete examples of different random component choices.

This is precisely why this introductory chapter, despite covering seemingly abstract theoretical material, forms the essential and non-negotiable foundation for the entire generalized linear models portion of this exam.

When an interaction improves in-sample fit but fails to improve, or even worsens, out-of-sample validation performance, that is a classic sign the added complexity is fitting noise in the training data rather than a genuine, generalizable relationship that will hold up on new data.

This produces one interaction column per non-base level of the categorical factor, allowing the numeric predictor's slope to differ across each level relative to the base level's slope.

Practice Test 31 Answer Key

  1. The correct answer is C (the interaction adds many additional coefficients that must each be credibly estimated): Interaction terms, especially between two categorical factors with several levels each, can add a large number of additional coefficients to estimate. Each of those coefficients needs enough supporting data volume to be estimated credibly; without it, the added complexity can produce unstable or noisy relativities for sparsely populated combinations. The actuary must weigh the potential improvement in fit and predictive accuracy against this added estimation risk and the practical cost of maintaining a more complex rating plan.
  2. The correct answer is D (the individual coefficient estimates for the two correlated predictors can become unstable and difficult to interpret): When two predictors are highly correlated, a condition known as multicollinearity, the design matrix contains largely redundant information about those predictors, making it statistically difficult to disentangle each predictor's individual effect on the response. This can produce coefficient estimates with inflated standard errors and unstable, sometimes counterintuitive, signs or magnitudes, even though the model's overall fitted values and predictive accuracy may remain reasonable despite this instability.
  3. The correct answer is D (the variance inflation factor, which quantifies how much a predictor's coefficient variance is inflated due): The variance inflation factor, commonly abbreviated VIF, is a standard diagnostic specifically designed to detect multicollinearity by measuring how much a given predictor's coefficient variance is inflated because of its linear association with the other predictors already in the model. A high VIF for a predictor signals that its individual effect may be difficult to estimate reliably alongside the other correlated predictors, prompting the actuary to consider removing or combining redundant variables.
  4. The correct answer is A (a deviance-based likelihood ratio test comparing the reduction in deviance to the added degree of freedom): For nested GLMs differing by a small number of parameters, the standard approach is a deviance-based likelihood ratio test, which compares the drop in deviance achieved by adding the predictor against a chi-squared reference distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of added parameters. A large enough reduction in deviance relative to that reference indicates the added predictor provides a statistically meaningful improvement rather than simply fitting to noise.
  5. The correct answer is A (an overly complex model risks overfitting the training data, producing unstable): A model with many predictors and interactions, especially relative to the amount of available data, can fit idiosyncratic patterns in the training sample that do not reflect genuine, generalizable relationships. This overfitting produces coefficients that may look statistically appealing in sample but perform poorly and lack credibility when applied to new policies, which is why predictor selection should balance statistical fit improvement against sample size, business rationale, and out-of-sample validation performance.

Penalized criteria like AIC and BIC, or holdout validation itself, exist precisely to guard against this tradeoff.

Criteria like AIC and BIC explicitly add a penalty term for the number of parameters to counteract this tendency. The senior actuary's caution reflects the well established fit-versus-complexity tradeoff central to model selection.

A quasi-Poisson approach instead keeps the Poisson mean structure but rescales the variance by an estimated dispersion factor without specifying a complete distribution, so it lacks a true likelihood function. Practice Test 35 Answer Key

  1. The correct answer is A (The observed severity for that claim is much lower than the model's fitted value, an unusual case): A large negative deviance residual indicates that a claim's observed value falls substantially below what the model predicted, contributing disproportionately to the total deviance. Since nearly all other residuals cluster within a narrower range, this particular claim stands out as an unusual case worth investigating further. It could reflect a genuine unusual claim, a data entry issue, or a missing explanatory variable, but the residual itself does not confirm which explanation applies. Investigating outliers like this is a standard part of GLM diagnostic review, not something to be dismissed automatically.
  2. The correct answer is B (Approximately negative 1.79, indicating the observed count fell below the model's fitted expectation): The raw residual is 1 minus 5.0, which equals negative 4.0. Dividing this by the square root of the fitted value, the square root of 5.0 being approximately 2.236, gives a Pearson residual of about negative 1.79. The negative sign confirms the observed claim count was lower than the model predicted for this policy. A residual of this magnitude is noticeable but not extreme, and would typically be reviewed alongside other diagnostics rather than treated as a severe outlier on its own.
  3. The correct answer is D (Consider a negative binomial or quasi-Poisson model, since a ratio well above 1.0 signals overdispersion): A dispersion ratio near 1.0 is expected under a correctly specified Poisson model, so a value of 3.4 indicates the observed variance substantially exceeds what the Poisson assumption predicts. This is a classic sign of overdispersion, often caused by unobserved heterogeneity among policyholders that the Poisson model does not capture. A negative binomial model directly models this extra variance through an additional parameter, while a quasi-Poisson approach rescales the variance estimate without changing the mean structure. Simply changing the link function or removing variables does not directly address the underlying source of overdispersion.
  4. The correct answer is C (The model may be somewhat overfit, performing better on training data than on unseen data): Training error reflects how well a model fits the exact data it was estimated on, while cross-validation error estimates performance on data the model has not seen during that fold's training. A meaningful gap between the two, with training error notably lower, is a common signature of overfitting, where the model has partly captured noise specific to the training sample. This does not necessarily mean the cross-validation procedure was implemented incorrectly, since some gap is expected even for reasonably well fit models. The size of the gap is what actuaries examine to judge whether the model generalizes acceptably.
  5. This consistent dominance indicates Model A more effectively separates high risk from low risk policies throughout the portfolio, not just at a single decile. The comparison is valid even when the two models use different variables, since lift charts evaluate predictive ranking rather than model structure directly. This result says nothing directly about which model has a higher or lower AIC.

The deviance residual instead is the signed square root of that observation's contribution to the total deviance, based directly on the likelihood, and the two need not have the same magnitude for a given observation.

A larger area means the model's risk ranking more effectively concentrates actual outcomes, such as losses, among policies predicted to be highest risk. This measure of discrimination is independent of the number of parameters in the model and does not directly indicate statistical significance of coefficients. It complements, rather than replaces, fit statistics like deviance when evaluating a model's overall usefulness.

Since 90.0 is far larger than the critical value of 11.07 at the 5% significance level, the actuary rejects the null hypothesis that all five rating variable coefficients are zero. This provides strong evidence that the rating variables meaningfully improve the model over the intercept-only baseline.

In such cases it is reasonable for the actuary to consider practical factors such as how easily the model's variables can be explained to stakeholders, how stable the coefficients are across different samples, and how the model performs on holdout data. A small AIC gap does not invalidate either model, nor does it call for arbitrarily altering the penalty constant used in AIC's definition. This kind of judgment call is common when statistical criteria alone do not clearly separate candidate models.
  10. This dependence on evaluation order is a well recognized limitation of stepwise procedures rather than a fundamental flaw that prevents their use altogether. The deviance statistic remains well defined even in the presence of correlated predictors. Correlation affects which variable stepwise selection happens to choose, not whether either variable's coefficient can be validly estimated.

Examining deviance residuals from held-out cross-validation folds instead shows how the model behaves on data it never saw during that fold's estimation, offering a more honest picture of generalization. This approach does not guarantee residuals will be smaller, nor does it eliminate the need to separately check for overdispersion. It provides a complementary, more realistic diagnostic than training-based residuals alone.

These two formulas generally produce similar values for most observations but can diverge more noticeably for extreme or poorly fit observations. This divergence is expected mathematically and does not indicate an error in either calculation. Deviance residuals are valid for Poisson and other exponential family distributions, not only for the normal distribution.

This understatement makes p-values appear smaller than they should be, increasing the risk of concluding a variable is statistically significant when it is not. Correcting for overdispersion, through a negative binomial model or a quasi-Poisson dispersion adjustment, produces standard errors that better reflect the true variability in the data. This issue arises regardless of which link function, such as log, is used in the model.

This result is empirical and specific to the data at hand, so it does not establish that the log link is theoretically correct for every Poisson claim frequency application in general. The alternative link function model is not proven invalid, only less predictive in this particular comparison.

Presenting both gives management an intuitive picture alongside a concise numerical benchmark, rather than duplicating identical information. Neither tool replaces fit statistics like deviance or AIC, since those measure goodness of fit rather than risk discrimination.

This diagnostic targets specific variables in a way that an overall fitted-value plot cannot.

With 250,000 policies that penalty is substantial, so BIC will more aggressively reject additional parameters that only marginally improve fit, which many actuaries consider desirable protection against overfitting in very large datasets.

The appropriate response is investigation rather than an automatic action, since blindly deleting or reacting to a single flagged point risks discarding real information or masking a modeling deficiency.

AIC is oriented toward minimizing prediction error and can be shown to be asymptotically efficient for that goal, while BIC is oriented toward identifying a parsimonious approximation of the underlying process. The correct answer is C (Pearson residuals scale the raw difference by the standard deviation, deviance residuals use the log likelihood): The Pearson residual for an observation is the raw difference between the observed and fitted value divided by the square root of the assumed variance function evaluated at the fitted mean, mirroring the classical standardized residual from linear regression. The deviance residual instead takes the signed square root of that observation's contribution to the total deviance statistic, which is derived directly from the log likelihood rather than from a variance-scaled difference. The two residuals coincide exactly only for the normal distribution and can diverge meaningfully for skewed families like Poisson or gamma, especially for observations with small fitted means.

The correct answer is B (Unobserved heterogeneity across policyholders inflates variance, and a negative binomial or quasi-Poisson model corrects it): Overdispersion in claim count data commonly arises because policyholders within the same rating cells still differ in unobserved risk characteristics, so the true variance of claim counts exceeds the mean even though the Poisson distribution forces variance to equal the mean. A negative binomial GLM introduces an extra parameter that lets variance exceed the mean directly, while a quasi-Poisson approach keeps the Poisson mean structure but rescales the standard errors by the estimated dispersion factor. Both remedies preserve the interpretable mean structure of the original model rather than discarding data or switching to an entirely different link.

The correct answer is D (Stepwise selection can settle on a locally optimal subset since it never revisits earlier skipped combinations): Because forward stepwise selection commits to each added variable and never revisits alternative combinations it declined earlier in the process, it can converge to a model that is only locally optimal rather than the truly best-fitting subset of a given size. A variable pair that individually contributes little deviance improvement but is jointly powerful in combination can be missed entirely if neither one is selected early on its own merit. Backward elimination and hybrid stepwise procedures can reach different final models from the same starting data, which is itself evidence that stepwise procedures are not guaranteed to find a single globally optimal answer.

The correct answer is D (Cross validation measures held-out performance directly, while AIC estimates it analytically from in-sample fit plus a penalty): Cross validation empirically estimates out-of-sample performance by repeatedly holding out actual data, fitting the model on the remainder, and measuring error on the excluded portion, giving a direct simulation of how the model would perform on new policies. AIC instead estimates that same generalization quality analytically, using the full in-sample log likelihood adjusted by a penalty term that approximates the expected optimism from fitting to the same data being evaluated. Both target the same underlying concept of out-of-sample predictive quality, but cross validation trades additional computation time for an estimate that does not rely on the asymptotic approximations AIC's penalty term is built on.

The correct answer is A (Deviance always favors the largest model since adding any variable can only improve in-sample fit): Because the maximum likelihood estimation procedure can always adjust an added variable's coefficient toward zero if that variable has no genuine relationship with the response, adding any variable can never make the in-sample deviance worse and will typically improve it slightly just from fitting sampling noise. If model selection relied on residual deviance alone, it would therefore always favor the largest available model regardless of whether the additional variables generalize to new data, a classic overfitting failure. AIC and BIC address this by explicitly subtracting a penalty proportional to the number of parameters, so that a variable must improve fit by more than the size of its penalty to be worth including.

A bidirectional stepwise procedure re-evaluates every variable currently in the model at each step and can remove one whose contribution has become insignificant once other variables are present, giving it more flexibility than either pure forward or pure backward selection alone. This bidirectional flexibility still does not guarantee finding the single best possible subset, since the procedure remains a sequential search rather than an exhaustive comparison of every combination.

The correct answer is D (Negative binomial has variance rising quadratically in the mean; quasi-Poisson just rescales Poisson standard errors): The negative binomial distribution is a genuine probability model in its own right, with a variance function that grows quadratically in the mean rather than equaling it, which changes both the coefficient point estimates and their standard errors relative to a plain Poisson fit. A quasi-Poisson adjustment, by contrast, keeps the exact same Poisson mean structure and coefficient estimates but multiplies every standard error by the square root of the estimated dispersion parameter, correcting inference without introducing a new likelihood. Because quasi-Poisson is not a full likelihood, it cannot be compared across models using AIC or BIC in the usual way, while the negative binomial model can.

The coefficient itself is not an additive claim count difference, which would only apply under an identity link. It also does not describe a share of total portfolio claims, which is an entirely different quantity. This is actually a strength of the Tweedie approach, not a limitation. Convergence speed depends on data size and model complexity rather than being uniformly faster for either approach. A Tweedie model combines both effects into a single pure premium mean and does not natively decompose them into separate frequency and severity outputs. Both GLM approaches, not neither, are capable of producing this kind of rating variable insight when structured appropriately. Generalized additive models are a separate technique choice and are not required simply to obtain frequency and severity diagnostics.

Dividing by only some of the known factors or adding a flat adjustment instead of dividing does not correctly invert the multiplicative structure. This is the same algebra used to back out an implied relativity from a filed rate table.

Option A skips the required division into $100 units, which would produce a wildly overstated result. Option B ignores the insured value entirely and treats the rate factors as a stand-alone dollar premium. Option C incorrectly sums the two relativities instead of multiplying them together as the plan requires.

Nothing in the relativities alone establishes that the two categories are statistically identical, which would require comparing confidence intervals or a formal hypothesis test. A relativity of 1.48 is a multiplicative factor, not a fixed dollar amount, so it does not mean claims cost exactly 48 dollars more. Differing relativities are actually evidence against merging commute use into the base category, not a reason to do so.
  33. There is no mathematical guarantee that brick construction will land below 1.0, since its relativity depends entirely on the fitted data. Other construction types still need their own relativities reported in the rating plan regardless of which level is the base. Choosing a base level does not change the underlying distributional assumption used to fit the GLM.
  34. The correct answer is B (The combined effect of both variables together differs from summing their separate main effects): An interaction term captures how the joint effect of two variables departs from what would be predicted by simply adding their individual main effects together, and a nonzero interaction coefficient signals that this departure is present in the fitted data. A significant interaction term is a reason to keep, not remove, both underlying variables from the model. The interaction coefficient does not by itself say anything about whether vehicle age has an independent main effect, which is captured by its own separate coefficient. A negative sign on an interaction term reflects the direction of the combined effect and is not evidence of a data problem.
  35. The correct answer is D (The new GLM separates high-risk from low-risk policies more effectively): A higher Gini index reflects a greater ability to rank-order policies by risk, meaning the new model does a better job of distinguishing high-risk from low-risk policies compared to the existing rating plan on the same holdout data. The Gini index measures discriminatory power and says nothing directly about the overall average premium level charged. It is not tied to the number of rating variables in the model, since a model with fewer or more variables could achieve a similarly high Gini. The Gini index is specifically designed for this kind of rating plan comparison, which is exactly why it was computed here.
  36. The correct answer is A (To confirm the variable actually relates to expected loss potential): Regulators typically require documented actuarial rationale to confirm that a rating variable reflects a genuine relationship to expected loss or expense rather than merely correlating with an unrelated demographic or proxy factor. This requirement is about actuarial justification, not about minimizing premium levels for any particular group of policyholders. Documentation cannot guarantee statistical significance, which is a property of the fitted data rather than something a written rationale can create. There is no fixed regulatory limit on the number of variables in a plan simply because of this documentation requirement.
  37. The correct answer is C (A single combined model reduces modeling workload for a smaller book): Fitting and maintaining one Tweedie pure premium model instead of two separate frequency and severity models reduces the overall workload, which is a practical advantage for an insurer with limited resources and a smaller book of business. Tweedie models do not inherently require more data than fitting two separate GLMs, and in some cases can be estimated with less. Standard holdout validation techniques apply equally well to Tweedie models as to separate frequency and severity models. Accuracy depends on how well each approach fits the actual claims experience, not on an inherent advantage of the Tweedie structure.
  38. The correct answer is B (The rider age discount outweighs the displacement surcharge in this case): Multiplying 600 by 1.25 and then by 0.75 gives 562.50, which is below the 600 base rate because the rider age relativity's proportional discount is larger than the displacement relativity's proportional surcharge once both are combined. The base rate itself is a fixed plan-level value and is not individually recalculated for a single policyholder. Multiplicative relativities can absolutely combine to a value below 1.0 overall when a discount factor outweighs a surcharge factor, so this outcome is expected rather than impossible. There is no indication in the scenario that any relativity was applied more than once.
  39. The relativity is a rate factor rather than a hard cap on the resulting premium, which also depends on the base rate and other applicable factors. It reflects modeled loss cost differences, not simply employee headcount at each business type. A relativity above 2.0 is not inherently evidence of a data error, since genuinely large loss cost differences between hazard classes are common in commercial liability lines.
  40. The correct answer is D (It gives a stable, precise reference point for other relativities): A good base level choice should remain a large and stable segment of the book over time, since a reference group with substantial underlying data produces a more stable and precisely estimated baseline that other relativities are measured against. There is no guarantee that other relativities will all exceed 1.0, since some levels could plausibly have lower expected loss cost than the base. Choosing a base level does not remove the need to test statistical significance for the variable as a whole. Choosing which level serves as the reference does not force any variable to be treated as continuous.
  41. It also does not describe the probability of any single future policy's frequency, which is a different kind of statement entirely. The interval is a statement about the coefficient estimate itself, not about the dollar premiums charged to individual policyholders. Since the interval from 0.28 to 0.52 excludes zero, it does support the estimate being meaningfully different from no effect.

Here e to the 0.15 equals 1.162, meaning this level is about 16.2 percent higher than the base level. Reading the coefficient itself as the relativity, or adding one to it, skips the exponentiation the log link requires. This is exactly how a filed rate table's relativities are derived from a fitted GLM's coefficient table.

A close statewide average does not by itself validate the model, since offsetting regional errors can mask a real structural problem. This kind of regional pattern does not automatically mean the model should be discarded, since a targeted fix like adding a geographic variable may resolve it. The Gini index measures overall risk differentiation and is not necessarily poor just because regional bias exists.

Here e to the -0.2 equals 0.819, meaning this level is about 18.1 percent lower than the base level. Reading the coefficient itself as the relativity, or adding one to it, skips the exponentiation the log link requires. This is exactly how a filed rate table's relativities are derived from a fitted GLM's coefficient table.
  45. The correct answer is A (Rating variables should be reasonably transparent about risk): Regulators commonly expect insurers to be able to explain, at least in general terms, how a rating variable relates to expected risk of loss, even when the underlying scoring methodology itself remains a vendor's proprietary trade secret. This does not mean the full formula must be made public, since confidentiality of the exact algorithm can often be preserved while still providing a general risk rationale. Proprietary third-party scores are not automatically prohibited outright, and many jurisdictions permit their use subject to this kind of disclosure expectation. The insurer is not required to abandon vendor-based scoring entirely simply because full transparency of the formula is not required.

Practice Test 43 Answer Key

  1. The correct answer is C (Separate frequency and severity models isolate each driver's effect): Building distinct frequency and severity models produces two separate sets of coefficients, which directly shows whether hazard class drives frequency, whether wage and benefit levels drive severity, or both, matching the actuary's stated goal. A Tweedie model's combined mean structure does not natively decompose which driver affects which underlying component of pure premium. Both frequency-severity and Tweedie approaches can, with proper structuring, provide useful rating insight, so it is not accurate that neither approach offers any isolation at all. Combining two conceptually different drivers into a single variable would blur rather than isolate their individual effects on frequency and severity.
  2. Summing the relativities and base rate together, as in option A, does not correspond to how multiplicative GLM-based rating plans are structured. Dividing by each relativity, as in option B, would invert the intended direction of both the credit and the surcharge. Taking the difference between the two relativities, as in option C, discards the base rate's role entirely and does not reflect the filed methodology.
  3. The correct answer is B (The long-haul relativity is more precisely estimated than the intermediate relativity): A narrow confidence interval reflects a more precise estimate, so the long-haul relativity's narrow interval indicates it is more precisely estimated than the intermediate relativity, whose wide interval reflects greater uncertainty, likely due to a smaller amount of underlying data. The two relativities are not equally reliable simply because both came from the same fitted model, since precision can genuinely differ by level. A wide confidence interval alone is not sufficient justification to automatically merge the intermediate level into the base category without further analysis. A relativity near 1.0 can still reflect a real, if modest, difference from the base and does not by itself prove the variable lacks predictive value overall.
  4. The correct answer is B (The middle payroll band, since it has the largest stable data share): Standard practice favors selecting the most heavily populated level as the base, since it offers the most stable and precisely estimated reference point for the relativities of every other band. Smaller payroll bands are not inherently lower risk simply due to their size, and this is not the actuarial rationale for base level selection in any case. Payroll size being conceptually continuous does not mean the choice of base level for the banded categorical variable is arbitrary, since data concentration still matters. Choosing the smallest band would not meaningfully simplify the relativity table's structure, which still requires a relativity for every remaining band regardless of which one is the base.
  5. The correct answer is C (The training program is linked to meaningfully lower claim severity): A negative coefficient under a log link means the exponentiated multiplicative effect is below 1.0, indicating lower expected claim severity for policies with the training program, and the low p-value indicates this reduction is statistically meaningful rather than likely due to chance. The program lowering expected severity does not amount to a guarantee that no severe claims will ever occur under it. A negative sign is a normal and valid outcome in a fitted coefficient and does not by itself indicate an error. This coefficient comes from a severity model and says nothing directly about claim frequency, which would be assessed in a separate frequency model.
  6. The correct answer is A (The model differentiates risk well and predicts accurately out of sample): Monotonically increasing bands show the model successfully rank-orders risk from low to high, while actual results tracking closely with predictions in each band shows the model's predictions are also accurate on data it was not fitted to, together supporting both good discrimination and good calibration. Monotonicity across bands is actually a desirable, expected property of a well-built model rather than a red flag. Passing this kind of validation test supports actuarial soundness but does not by itself satisfy every separate regulatory filing requirement, which typically involves additional documentation. The close tracking was described across all bands, not only the lowest one, so the favorable result applies broadly rather than to a single band.
  7. The correct answer is D (Rates must be adequate but not excessive relative to the risk they cover): A core ratemaking principle requires that overall rates be adequate to cover expected losses, expenses, and a reasonable profit provision, while also not being excessive relative to that underlying risk, which is exactly the demonstration the regulator is requesting. Regulators do not require identical rates across competing insurers, since rate levels can legitimately differ based on each company's own experience and expenses. There is no regulatory requirement tying rate approval to the specific software platform used to build the GLM. Maximizing underwriting profit within allowed limits is not the guiding principle here, since the excessive rate standard exists specifically to prevent overly high profit-driven pricing.
  8. The correct answer is B (A separate severity model allows its own heavy-tailed distribution choice): Building a standalone severity model lets the actuary select a distribution, such as a gamma or a more heavy-tailed alternative, specifically suited to severity's behavior, independent of whatever distributional assumption governs the frequency model. A Tweedie model's single combined mean structure does not separately expose a distinct heavy-tailed severity assumption the way two standalone models can. Both frequency-severity and Tweedie approaches, when properly specified, can incorporate appropriate distributional choices, so it is inaccurate to say neither permits this. Frequency and severity models are not required to share the same distributional family, since they represent fundamentally different kinds of random variables.

Option B incorrectly sums the two adjustment factors rather than multiplying them, which does not reflect how these factors are combined under standard workers compensation rating rules. Here that is e to the (0.5 minus 0.25), or e to the 0.25, which equals 1.284, about 28.4 percent apart. Subtracting on the log scale and then exponentiating correctly undoes the log link. Taking a raw ratio of coefficients has no meaningful interpretation under a log-link GLM.

The fitted data in this scenario shows the urban relativity higher than the suburban relativity, so the reverse ordering suggested in option B does not match the stated results. There is no fixed rule that all territory relativities in a rating plan must fall within a 0.5 to 1.5 range, since genuinely large risk differences can exceed that range. This flexibility is a key practical advantage of the frequency-severity approach in classification ratemaking.
